MEMORANDUM

       To:    Members of the Village of Plain City Council
       From: Haley Lupton, Village Administrator
       Date: July 6, 2026
       RE:    Resolution 25-2026: Authorizing and Directing the Village Administrator to Apply to
              the Ohio Public Works Commission for Clean Ohio Green Space Conservation
              Program Funds



Background:

Village staff has begun preparations to apply to the grant funding opportunity administered by the
Ohio Public Works Commission (“OPWC”) for the Clean Ohio Green Space Conservation Program.
The program provides up to 75% reimbursement assistance for local government subdivisions for
eligible land acquisition or improvement projects. Staff is preparing an application for financial
assistance to complete improvements to the Sugar Run Park. The Village did receive financial
assistance in 2025 to acquire the aforementioned property through the same OPWC grant
program. Staff believes this program is an excellent opportunity to request additional financial
assistance in order to complete the Sugar Run Improvement Project in a fiscally responsible and
efficient manner.

In addition to the above project, staff is preparing an application for financial assistance for the
Darby Land Acquisition Project. This project, if approved, would provide funding to purchase the
approximately 6.77 acres along the Big Darby Creek and adjacent to Smucker Park and place such
land in a state of conservation and available for public and recreational use.

Required by the OPWC, to be submitted with the applications, is a legislative resolution of
authorization from the Village Council that authorizes and directs the Village Administrator to
complete and submit an application for funding. As such, staff is requesting Council’s review and
approval of Resolution 25-2026 to be able to submit the aforementioned applications.




        800 Village Boulevard | P.O. Box 167 | Plain City, OH 43064 | 614-873-3527 | plaincityohio.gov


Objective:

To authorize the Village Administrator to apply to the Clean Ohio Green Space Conservation
Program as administered by the OPWC in order to request funding for the Sugar Run
Improvement Project and the Darby Land Acquisition Project.

Recommendation:

Staff supports and recommends the passage of Resolution 25-2026 at the second reading on
August 10, 2026. The submittal of an application for financial assistance furthers the goals of
Council and, if said application is approved, will provide necessary funding to complete vital
improvements at the Sugar Run Park and protect and conserve land along the Big Darby Creek
through the Darby Land Acquisition Project.




        800 Village Boulevard | P.O. Box 167 | Plain City, OH 43064 | 614-873-3527 | plaincityohio.gov

ADMINISTRATOR TO APPLY TO THE OHIO PUBLIC WORKS COMMISSION FOR
     CLEAN OHIO GREEN SPACE CONSERVATION PROGRAM FUNDS

WHEREAS, the Ohio Public Works Commission (“OPWC”) administers financial assistance
for environmental conservation projects through the Clean Ohio Green Space Conservation

WHEREAS, the Village Council desires financial assistance through the Clean Ohio Green

MEMORANDUM

       To:    Members of the Village of Plain City Council
       From: Haley Lupton, Village Administrator
       Date: June 23, 2026
       RE:    Resolution 26-2026: Adopting the 2026 Plain City Comprehensive Plan Update



Background:

Pursuant to the direction of the Village Council, staff has engaged with the qualified consultant,
MKSK Studios, to complete thorough updates to the 2018 Plain City Comprehensive Plan. Through
exceptional research, public engagement, and stakeholder interviews, the finalized 2026 Plain
City Comprehensive Plan Update has been completed and is available for Council review and
adoption, if Council so desires. The finalized version of the plan is attached to Resolution 26-2026
in the form of Exhibit A. The plan advances and completes the Village Council goal of “continued
focus on smart planning and due diligence in regards to Village growth”.

Objective:

To adopt the 2026 Plain City Comprehensive Plan Update.

Recommendation:

Staff supports and recommends the passage of Resolution 26-2026 at the second reading on
August 10, 2026. The 2026 Plain City Comprehensive Plan has been completed through extensive
research and stakeholder input. Staff believes the plan will continue to support the Village
Council and staff in future decision-making and provides vital methodologies and
recommendations regarding a variety of influential topics affecting the Village.

4 PLAIN CITY COMPREHENSIVE PLAN


                          Letter from the Mayor
                          Jody Carney
                          What an exciting time it is to be in Plain City!

                          Over the past year and a half, our community has come together
                          in thoughtful and intentional ways to shape a shared vision for our
                          future. This process has been rooted in meaningful conversations, and I
am truly grateful to everyone who took the time to participate. Every response, whether shared
in person or online, has played an important role in guiding this plan.

At our community workshops, I had the opportunity to meet many of you face to face and hear
directly what makes Plain City so special. Those conversations left a lasting impression on me.
Time and again, I heard how much you value our community character, our small-town pride,
and the sense of connection that defines this Village. Those priorities are not going away. In
fact, they have guided this plan from the very beginning.

We made a clear commitment to honor Plain City’s rich history while also embracing fresh
ideas, the realities of a growing Central Ohio region, and the unique opportunities ahead. There
is no doubt that growth brings complex challenges, but throughout this process, the Village has
remained mindful of all who call Plain City home.

As a farm girl growing up, I understand the importance of agricultural roots and the
responsibility we carry to preserve them. At the same time, I recognize the need to adapt
and plan for the future. Plain City represents a special balance of both. We are committed to
maintaining our agricultural heritage while investing in infrastructure, supporting thoughtful
growth, and making local decisions that benefit residents of all ages.

This Comprehensive Plan serves as a guide for that work. It reflects our shared values,
strengthens partnerships, and helps us make informed decisions about where and how we grow.
It identifies opportunities, sets priorities, and ensures that our actions align with the vision you
helped create.

This is also a living document. As our community evolves, so too will this plan, allowing us to
respond to new challenges and opportunities with care and purpose.

The best is yet to come. Together, we are building a future that respects our past, reflects who
we are, and prepares Plain City for generations to come.

With gratitude,

Mayor Jody Carney
Village of Plain City


                                                                               INTRODUCTION 5


        INTRODUCTION
        Reflecting on Plain City’s past, outlining the
        planning process, and framing the unique
        moment shaping the Village’s next chapter.
        Plain City is at a defining moment. Long known for its rural character, strong
        community values, and small-town feel, the Village is now experiencing
        steady growth shaped by new development, expanding infrastructure, and
        regional change across Central Ohio. These shifts bring opportunity—but also
        responsibility.

        Plain City has planned before. The 2018 Comprehensive Plan established a
        foundation for managing growth and protecting the qualities that make the
        community unique. Since then, conditions have evolved. Population growth
        has accelerated, infrastructure investments are underway, and the Village
        is preparing for a transition to city status later this decade. Together, these
        changes signal the need to look ahead once again.

        The Picture Plain City Comprehensive Plan Update is a continuation of that
        legacy of foresight. It asks important questions about how and where the
        Village grows, how infrastructure and amenities keep pace, and how Plain City
        can welcome new opportunities without losing its identity. Most importantly,
        it reflects the voices of residents, business owners, and stakeholders who care
        deeply about the future of this community.

        Planning is how communities take ownership of change. This
        Comprehensive Plan Update provides a clear, community-driven framework
        to guide growth, investment, and decision-making, ensuring that as Plain City
        evolves, it remains rooted in the values that make it special.

                                                                                           INTRODUCTION 9


PLAN PROCESS
Community Understanding
The plan process began with a thorough assessment
of Plain City’s existing physical, demographic and
economic conditions and the community’s relative
position in Central Ohio. This included a community
tour and audit, Advisory Committee kick-off meeting,
Community Workshop, stakeholder interviews, and
existing conditions analysis. This baseline understanding
of Plain City resulted in a series of maps and analysis
findings, as well as a communications and engagement
plan. These assets set a course for a robust community-
driven planning process tailored to the unique needs and
aspirations of Plain City.

Community Visioning
The visioning process invited residents and business
owners to think big about the future of Plain City,
helping the Planning Team understand what matters
most to the community. Input gathered through
Community Open Houses and Advisory Committee
meetings shaped the planning principles and community
priorities that guide this Plan Update. Building on that
foundation, Village Staff Workshops refined ideas from
the 2018 Comprehensive Plan, including placemaking,
land use, development, and transportation, into clear,
actionable recommendations.

Synthesis
Building on the community review and direction of           Conditions & Trends
the planning process, the visioning, strategies and plan
concepts were synthesized into a complete document.
The Comprehensive Plan Update was then reviewed
                                                               Assessment
                                                                 In support of the Comprehensive Plan Update for Plain City, Ohio
by the community and the planning and zoning
commission before being adopted by Village Council.

                                                                INTRODUCTION 11


PLAN CONTEXT
The Village of Plain City is located in central Ohio at
the intersection of Union County and Madison County,
20 miles northwest of Columbus. The Village sits along
key regional corridors, including U.S. Route 33, U.S.
Route 42, and State Route 161, that connect it to nearby
communities and employment centers such as Dublin,
Marysville, and Columbus. These connections place Plain
City at the edge of one of the country's fastest-growing
metropolitan areas, where suburban growth transitions to
the agricultural landscapes that continue to characterize
the Village and its surroundings.

The Village is surrounded by a mix of rural townships,
                                                              New housing developments in Plain City are the result
growing suburban communities, and emerging
                                                            of regional growth. The Madison Meadows subdivision is
employment areas. Commercial and institutional growth                                located in southwest Plain City.
along SR-161 and Industrial Parkway has expanded
nearby economic activity, while farmland and open space
remain a defining feature of the surrounding landscape.
Plain City is also located within the watershed of Big
Darby Creek, one of Ohio’s most ecologically significant
waterways. Tributaries of the creek pass through the
community, placing environmental stewardship at the
center of long-term land use decisions.

Infrastructure systems and regional relationships will
also shape the Village’s future. The Mid-Ohio Water &
Sewer District is planning new water and wastewater
infrastructure serving Plain City and portions of
Madison County. These investments may enable new
development in areas surrounding the Village and could
generate future annexation requests as landowners
seek municipal services. Nearby communities are also
planning for growth, and infrastructure and land use
                                                              Plain City is shaped by its rural character and proximity
decisions in cities like Dublin and Marysville will          to the Big Darby Creek and its tributaries. Smucker Park
impact Plain City. Together, these overlapping systems,     (pictured) is one of the Village's newest parks, located in
transportation, utilities, environmental resources, and                                                   the southern .
neighboring jurisdictions place Plain City in a unique
position to guide growth, coordinate with regional
partners, and protect the natural and community assets
that define the Village.

History                                                     As development pressures increase and infrastructure
                                                            investments expand, Plain City is at a pivotal moment
Originally the home to Wyandotte and Mingo Native
                                                            in its growth. Understanding who lives in the Village
American nations, the village plat for Plain City, then

                                                            The community snapshot on the following page offers

                                                            Update.
community as a growing center of stockyards and

In 1886 four Amish families arrived in the area and
established a congregation. The area's Amish and
Mennonite population then grew to more than 300
families by some estimates and the population was well-
established for nearly a century. Though much of the Old
Amish community left sometime after 1970, Amish and
Mennonite families and culture are still active parts of
community life today.

After the 1970s, the Village experienced new
development, mostly residential subdivision and some
highway-oriented development within the US 42
corridor. This suburban-type growth nearly doubled the           A long-standing tradition of agriculture, community
Village’s population between 1970 and the present. The          gathering, and local identity continues to shape Plain
21st century brought an influx of new housing, business         City, which remains deeply connected to its heritage.
growth, and public facilities, while Plain City remained
connected to its agricultural roots, preserving a strong
sense of community and small-town values that continue
to shape the Village.

Community Profile
Today, Plain City is home to approximately 4,916
residents within 4.4 square miles of land area. The
Village's development pattern reflects a mix of
established neighborhoods, emerging residential growth,
agricultural land, and a compact historic Uptown,
creating a distinct small-town character within a rapidly
urbanizing region.

                                                                                                                                                                                                INTRODUCTION 19


        COMMUNITY PROFILE
        This Plan Update is built on community
        insight that defines shared priorities and
        guides the Plan’s recommendations.
        Picture Plain City kicked off in April 2025 with a clear focus: to reconnect
        with where the Village has been since the 2018 Comprehensive Plan and
        to understand how this Plan Update can help guide Plain City’s future.
        Throughout this process, the central question remained the same, how can
        the 2026 Comprehensive Plan Update best prepare the community for what's
        next. This effort explored the right questions to ask the community and how
        those responses could meaningfully shape the plan’s recommendations.

        Community engagement began in June 2025 with the first Advisory
        Committee meeting, followed by the first community workshop in August.
        These early conversations focused on identifying key challenges and
        opportunities related to housing, economic growth, infrastructure, city services,
        and community identity.

        The engagement process included both in-person and digital conversations
        with residents, businesses, community organizations, and other stakeholders.
        By actively listening to a wide range of voices, the planning team gathered
        insights that helped shape the plan’s priorities and strategies.

        Grounded in meaningful community input and established planning
        principles, the Comprehensive Plan builds on Plain City’s values, vision,
        and previous planning efforts. It serves as a policy guide for Council,
        boards and commissions, and staff as they make decisions and invest in the
        Village’s future. This chapter highlights the engagement process, community
        feedback and previews the key findings, demonstrating how local voices
        directly informed the Plan Update and set the stage for Plain City’s growth,
        conservation, and evolution over the next decade and beyond.

INTRODUCTION 21


INTRODUCTION
The Comprehensive Plan Update was guided by an
internal and collaborative engagement process designed
to ensure that the voices of residents, businesses, and
community partners help shape the future of Plain City.
Throughout the process, the planning team worked
to understand both the opportunities emerging from
regional growth and the identity residents want to
preserve as the community evolves.

Engagement activities were designed to reach people in
multiple ways, combining in-person conversations with
digital tools that allowed the community to participate
in their own way. Workshops, stakeholder discussions,
advisory committee meetings, and online engagement
helped capture a broad range of perspectives.

This chapter provided an overview of how the
engagement process unfolded and what was learned
along the way. It began with a snapshot of participation
and a summary of the planning process, followed by
the key themes that emerged from conversations with
the community. Together, these insights helped shape
the priorities and recommendations that guide the
Comprehensive Plan and reflect Plain City’s shared
vision for the future.

                                                                                direction of the Comprehensive Plan.

                                                      INTRODUCTION 27


KEY THEMES
Throughout the engagement process, the community shared priorities, concerns, and ideas for the Village’s future.
Clear themes began to emerge, revealing what matters most to the community. The following page highlights these
ideas, which directly informed the plan’s focus and recommendations.


              Rural landscapes and natural systems define Plain City’s identity, but continued growth puts these
              assets at risk. Expansion toward environmentally sensitive areas, both within the Village and through
              less coordinated development in surrounding townships, could gradually diminish farmland, tree cover,
              and ecological systems such as Big Darby Creek. Conservation tools, environmental stewardship, and
              coordinated land use planning can help protect these landscapes while guiding responsible growth.

              Plain City’s parks and recreation system is essential to creating strong community connections and
              shared spaces. Continued investment in new recreation options, park upgrades, and family‑focused
              amenities can enhance daily life, boost participation, and encourage healthier lifestyles. By improving
              accessibility and expanding programs, the Village can support a more active and connected community.

              Transportation infrastructure restricts movement between neighborhoods, parks, and regional
              destinations. Expanding pedestrian infrastructure, bike facilities, and strengthening connections to
              Uptown, neighborhoods, and regional trails such as the Heritage Trail can create a safer and more
              connected network.

              Traffic volumes and roadway safety concerns are increasing as development expands along key
              corridors. Higher speeds and congestion impact safety and traffic flow. Coordinated roadway design,
              traffic calming strategies, and corridor planning can help maintain safe and efficient travel while
              protecting community character.

              Uptown serves as the cultural and economic heart of Plain City, yet significant opportunities for
              growth and revitalization remain. Strategic redevelopment and carefully planned infill can help
              strengthen the district as a vibrant, walkable destination, supporting local businesses and community
              life while still preserving the area’s distinctive historic character.

              Small-town character is one of Plain City’s greatest strengths, but new development could
              compromise this identity. Without intentional design standards, placemaking efforts, and smart
              growth policies, new growth can alter the Village’s character. Planning that emphasizes architectural
              compatibility, placemaking, and inviting public spaces can help ensure new development reflects the
              Village's small-town feel.




28 PLAIN CITY COMPREHENSIVE PLAN


   There is demand for civic spaces and services alongside community growth. Limited access to civic
   amenities such as childcare, community centers, and shared public spaces may reduce opportunities
   for community interaction and support services. Investment in civic facilities can strengthen social
   connections and enhance quality of life.

   Housing demand is increasing as regional growth reaches Plain City, creating pressure on the local
   housing supply. Without a balanced approach to development, housing may become less attainable for
   young families, professionals, and older residents. Guiding residential growth to expand choices while
   maintaining neighborhood character can support long-term affordability and stability.

   Economic development opportunities are increasing as the Village becomes more visible within
   the region. Without careful planning, new commercial growth could follow conventional suburban
   patterns that weaken the Village’s distinct character. Targeted investment in locally scaled retail, dining,
   and mixed-use development can strengthen the local economy and fill gaps in the market.

   Infrastructure systems must evolve to support continued growth and development. As population
   and activity increase, pressure on parking, utilities, and public services will rise. Coordinated
   infrastructure planning can ensure these systems support expected growth without compromising
   quality of service.

                                                                                             INTRODUCTION 29


        RECOMMENDATIONS
        Presents a clear set of goals, strategies,
        and actions to guide Plain City’s growth,
        investment, and preservation efforts.
        The recommendations in this chapter represent the culmination of months of
        listening, learning, and analyzing what matters most to Plain City. They are
        rooted first in the voices of residents, business owners, and stakeholders who
        shared their perspectives during the initial round of community engagement.
        Early community workshops and Advisory Committee meetings identified
        key opportunities and challenges related to growth, housing, economic
        development, parks, transportation, and public services. These ideas were then
        tested and refined through a second community workshop, ensuring that the
        strategies reflected the priorities and aspirations of the broader community.

        In addition to community input, the recommendations were informed by
        careful analysis of local data, including demographic trends, housing patterns,
        land use, and regional growth pressures. This evidence helped shape actionable
        strategies that are both realistic and forward-looking, providing the Village
        with a clear roadmap for growth, conservation, and investment.

        Taken together, the recommendations translate Plain City’s vision and values
        into concrete actions. They provide a framework to guide land use, strengthen
        neighborhoods, support local businesses, expand parks and trails, improve
        connectivity, and enhance governance. Each recommendation is designed to
        help the Village manage change thoughtfully, preserve its character, and build
        a resilient, vibrant, and connected community for years to come.

PLAN FRAMEWORK
Plain City’s Comprehensive Plan is more than a
collection of ideas, it is a blueprint for action that reflects
the community’s values, vision, and aspirations. The
recommendations presented in this chapter are organized
through a clear framework that connects Plain City’s
long-term vision with practical steps for implementation.
This structure helps translate the ideas and priorities
identified through the planning process into coordinated
actions that can guide decisions, investments, and
partnerships over time.

At the heart of the framework is a simple progression—
from vision to action. It begins with a shared vision for
the future of Plain City and is supported by a series of
plan pillars that represent the community’s major priority
areas. The goals, strategies, and recommendations within

                                  INTRODUCTION 33


        PLAN PILLARS
        The Pillars represent the central focus of the Comprehensive Plan. They articulate the key direction for
        Plain City’s future, a response to current conditions, community aspirations, and the opportunities ahead.
        These statements serve as the foundation for the plan’s goals, strategies, and recommendations.

                   Pursue Smart Growth & Land Stewardship
                   Guide growth in a way that balances development opportunities with preservation of Plain
                   City’s rural character, natural resources, and agricultural heritage. By strategically identifying
                   areas for new housing, commercial, and mixed-use development while protecting farmland,
                   environmentally sensitive areas, and key corridors, the Village can ensure that growth is both
                   sustainable and well-coordinated. This approach prioritizes proactive land use planning,
                   thoughtful annexation, and long-term stewardship to maintain the Village’s distinct identity
                   while supporting future residents and businesses.

                   Strengthen Our Homes & Neighborhoods
                   Plain City’s neighborhoods are the foundation of its character and quality of life. Offering
                   diverse and attainable housing options ensures that residents of all ages and life stages can find
                   a home in the Village. Efforts include maintaining and modernizing the existing housing stock,
                   addressing affordability and accessibility, and introducing new housing variety. Strengthening
                   neighborhoods reinforces community cohesion, encourages lifelong residency, and fosters a
                   welcoming environment for both new and long-term residents.

                   Grow Jobs & Local Business
                   Supporting local businesses, encouraging entrepreneurship, and attracting employment
                   opportunities are central to Plain City’s economic vitality. By leveraging the Village’s regional
                   connections, school system, and strategic location along major corridors, Plain City can nurture
                   small businesses, strengthen its commercial hubs, and align workforce development with
                   emerging regional opportunities. Economic growth should focus on generating year-round
                   activity, supporting locally owned businesses, and ensuring that new investment enhances both
                   the community’s character and its long-term fiscal sustainability.

                   Expand and Care for Our Parks
                   Parks, trails, and open spaces are essential to Plain City’s quality of life. By investing in new
                   parks, enhancing existing facilities, and expanding trails and greenways, the Village can provide
                   spaces for recreation, social connection, and environmental stewardship. Thoughtful planning
                   ensures that parks are accessible to all residents, linked to neighborhoods and Uptown, and
                   designed to meet evolving recreational needs. Caring for these spaces preserves the Village’s
                   natural and cultural assets while creating lasting community benefits.

                   Connect Our Community
                   A safe, accessible, and multimodal transportation network strengthens connectivity across
                   Plain City. Prioritizing pedestrian and bicycle infrastructure, enhancing roadway safety, and
                   integrating regional trail and transit connections ensures residents can move throughout the
                   Village efficiently and safely. These investments support everyday travel, recreation, and economic
                   activity, while also fostering social interaction and linking neighborhoods, parks, and Uptown.


34 PLAIN CITY COMPREHENSIVE PLAN


Build on Momentum in Uptown
Uptown is the heart of Plain City, and maintaining its vibrancy is critical to community
identity and economic vitality. By fostering mixed-use development, expanding public
spaces, and supporting active streetscapes, the Village can attract visitors, businesses, and
residents throughout the day. Strategic redevelopment, enhanced public gathering areas,
and complementary housing options can ensure Uptown remains a vibrant hub that blends
commerce, culture, and community life.

Support Community Services & Partners
Effective community services bring stability to Plain City’s future. By strengthening partnerships
with schools, nonprofits, public safety agencies, and regional organizations, the Village can
enhance program delivery, expand recreational and educational opportunities, and ensure
equitable access to resources. Supporting these partners allows the Village to respond proactively
to community needs, foster collaboration, and build resilient social networks that benefit
all residents.

Lead with Good Governance
Transparent, accountable, and collaborative governance ensures that Plain City can respond to
growth, manage resources effectively, and maintain public trust. By building internal capacity,
aligning staffing and processes with community priorities, and fostering open communication,
the Village can engage residents meaningfully, make informed decisions, and create policies that
reflect shared goals. Strong governance also strengthens the Village’s ability to coordinate with
regional partners and position Plain City for sustainable, long-term success.

        1.2 Strategic Sites & Edges
        Concept Plans for Key Growth Areas: Creates high-level plans for key sites and community edges to guide
        future development, infrastructure, and design.

        As Plain City grows, some sites will carry greater importance than others in shaping community character,
        economic value, and long-term identity. This action focuses on those strategic opportunity sites, where
        the Village should lead with a clear vision, establish the principles that define strong development, and
        communicate both high expectations and real
        opportunity to the development community.

        This plan identifies two priority concept areas:
        Sweeney Run and Creekview Commerce Park.
        Sweeney Run represents a major neighborhood
        addition at Uptown’s southern edge and an
        opportunity to integrate a new neighborhood
        pattern that reflects Plain City's small-town
        qualities through connected housing, trails,
        linear park space, tree-lined streets, and support
        for small-scale business activity. Creekview
        Commerce Park represents a different but
        equally important priority: a long-term
        employment and revenue strategy tied to the
        Village’s future fiscal independence. As Plain
        City grows toward cityhood, Creekview offers
        a critical opportunity to expand the income tax           Quarry Trails, Columbus, Ohio transforms a former

        These areas should strive to blend development

        objectives with economic strategy, community

        Sweeney Run should balance neighborhood
        growth with strong public space, trail connections, and thoughtful placemaking. Creekview should
        balance employment growth with environmental stewardship and foster a flexible site framework that
        can accommodate a range of employers over time. In both cases, the goal is to move beyond land use
        designations and establish a clear vision for how these areas should function, connect, and contribute to the
        broader community.

        More broadly, this recommendation establishes a planning model for how Plain City should approach
        future strategic areas. For sites that play a major role in shaping the Village’s identity, economy, or
        development pattern, the Village should lead with a clear vision and translate that vision into concept plans
        that guide infrastructure, design, and development expectations. In this way, Sweeney Run and Creekview
        Commerce Park serve not only as priority projects, but also examples of how Plain City can thoughtfully
        guide future growth.

Development Principles
A strong project in Plain City will…

• Fit the fabric. Reinforce the contextual position of
  the area with respect to neighborhood character;
  compatible scale, frontage, and materials.
• Integrate logically. Pair complementary uses
  vertically or horizontally to keep areas active
  throughout the day. Plan sites thoughtfully. Organize
  buildings, access, service, and parking to prioritize
  people first.
• Connect clearly. Extend streets, sidewalks, and
  paths to close gaps and link to regional trails and
  parks. Integrate usable, connected open spaces with
  amenities that encourage activity and community
                                                             Columbus Avenue Sandusky OH, Source: Doug Hinebaugh
  gathering.
• Protect the Big Darby Creek. Utilize stormwater
  and riparian best practices; avoid floodways and
  respect sensitive areas. Treat waterways as a valuable
  community asset.
• Accommodate for walking & biking. Include
  safe crossings, traffic calming, bike parking, shade,
  lighting, and wayfinding.
• Diversify housing. Deliver a range of types to match
  evolving, local needs.
• Strengthen Uptown. Reuse historic buildings,
  fill gaps, and add upper-story housing; coordinate
  hours/events with neighbors.
• Be infrastructure-ready. Before new development
  happens, make sure the necessary infrastructure            Big Darby Creek, Source: Anthony Sasson
  (roads, water, sewer, utilities, stormwater, etc.) is in
  place or planned.
• Show economic value. Add taxable value, local
  revenue generation, and job space without over-
  extending services.
• Celebrate and reinforce identity. Incorporate Plain
  City’s history, art, and branding in new architecture
  and public realm enhancements.

1.5 Future Land Use Map
Define the intended long-term use of land across the
community to inform zoning and development decisions.

As part of this Comprehensive Plan Update, the Village
has updated its Future Land Use Map to reflect an
updated long-term vision for how land should be used,
conserved, and developed across the community. The
map (on page 39) establishes the Plain City’s intended
areas of growth and preservation, translating broad goals
for neighborhoods, economic development, open space,
infrastructure, and community character into a place-
based framework.

The Future Land Use Map is informed by past and
future planning, helping the Village identify areas for
conservation, farmland retention, and environmentally
sensitive development. It provides Village leadership,
staff, residents, property owners, and the development
community with a shared understanding of how different
areas of Plain City are expected to function over
time, supporting consistent and coordinated decisions            SR 161
on growth, annexation, infrastructure, and public
investment.

It is important to distinguish the Future Land Use
Map from zoning. The map expresses the Village’s
long-range policy direction, while zoning translates that
direction into parcel-level regulations, permitted uses,
and development standards. The Future Land Use Map
serves as a foundation for future action, including zoning
updates, development review processes, annexation
decisions, and infrastructure planning. Together,
the Future Land Use Map and the Village's zoning
ordinances ensure that future change across Plain City
is intentional, flexible, and aligned with the community’s
long-term vision.

Agriculture
Agricultural areas include working farms, actively used
for agricultural activities, including; cultivated cropland,
pastures, and raising livestock. Agricultural areas may
include fence rows/tree rows, wooded areas, ponds, large
swales to drain cropland. These areas also support the
primary residence of the property owner and any out-
buildings associated with activities on the working farm.

Rural Residential
Rural Residential areas offer opportunities for low-
intensity development that is well-integrated with the
natural landscape and agricultural uses. Residential
development may occur as individual single-family
structures on large lots, or clusters of homes designed
to preserve large amounts of open space, which should
be interconnected. Future planned developments are
encouraged to incorporate low-impact development
and green infrastructure practices to minimize any
environmental impacts of impervious surfaces and
stormwater runoff.




 Plain City, Source: Google Earth                         Plain City, Source: Google Earth

Conservation Residential
Conservation developments ensure the preservation
of open space in the design of residential subdivisions.
A mix of residential types are clustered together to
preserve the maximum amount of open space. This
open space should be contiguous, publicly accessible,
and strategically placed to conserve natural and rural
elements and to promote connectivity for greenspace
systems and trails. Future planned developments are
encouraged to incorporate low-impact development
and green infrastructure practices to minimize any
environmental impacts of impervious surfaces and
stormwater runoff.

Mixed Residential
New residential development should include a mixture
of housing types to fulfill Plain City’s diverse housing
needs. Mixed residential neighborhoods may include
a variety of single-family (detached and attached) and
multi-family building types. Development should
be designed as a cohesive, connected neighborhood,
rather than isolated subareas. Development should
be high-quality and include common neighborhood
amenities and open space connections. Future planned
developments are encouraged to incorporate low-
impact development and green infrastructure practices
to minimize any environmental impacts of impervious
surfaces and stormwater runoff.

Traditional Residential
Traditional Residential is characterized primarily by
early and mid-20th Century single family homes. Parks
and places of worship are also present. Existing housing
stock should be preserved and improved; however,
there are opportunities for single-lot infill development,
which should be of compatible scale and character with
surrounding homes. Future planned developments are
encouraged to incorporate low-impact development
and green infrastructure practices to minimize any
environmental impacts of impervious surfaces and
stormwater runoff.

Uptown
Uptown is the community’s historic Village core and has
a unique identity from Plain City’s other commercial
and activity centers. Development vertically integrates
uses in attached buildings, including a close sidewalk
orientation. Preservation and revitalization of historic
structures is a key objective. Targeted redevelopment of
underutilized, non-historic sites should be sensitive to
the historic form and scale of the Uptown.

In-Town Corridor
A mix of uses along an important corridor within the
Village core. Development is organized with consistent
building setbacks to create a defined street edge. Parking
is located to the side or rear of buildings to keep the
frontage active. Access is managed through shared
driveways and consolidation of curb cuts where possible.
Signage follows consistent design standards to reinforce
the Village’s character. Pedestrian access is required, with
clear connections from sidewalks or shared use paths to
building entrances. Future planned developments are
encouraged to incorporate low-impact development
and green infrastructure practices to minimize any
environmental impacts of impervious surfaces and
stormwater runoff.

Gateway Corridor
A mixed-use corridor located along key entries into
the Village, characterized by predominantly non-
residential uses such as retail, grocery, and dining, with
opportunities for residential, office, medical, and flex
industrial uses as part of integrated developments.
These corridors are designed to balance economic
activity with preservation of the Village’s rural character,
requiring significant building setbacks to maintain
viewsheds and accommodate shared-use paths, landscape
buffers, naturalized open space, and future roadway
improvements. Development is organized to minimize
direct access onto SR 161 and US 42, instead utilizing
shared access points and an internal street network
to support safe and efficient circulation. Buildings are
oriented toward public frontages or internal streets,
with parking located to the side or rear of principal
buildings. Continuous pedestrian and trail connections,
coordinated site design, and consistent landscaping
and screening standards contribute to a cohesive
corridor appearance while reducing visual and traffic
impacts along these primary gateways. Future planned
developments are encouraged to incorporate low-
impact development and green infrastructure practices
to minimize any environmental impacts of impervious
surfaces and stormwater runoff.

Business/Industrial
A range of office, research and development, medical, flex
industrial, and light manufacturing uses. Development is
typically campus-style, with buildings organized around
internal streets, open spaces, and coordinated site design.
Buildings should incorporate high-quality architectural
design that reflects the Village’s rural character. Sites are
expected to include clear pedestrian connections and
integrated open space networks, with links to regional
trails where feasible. Stormwater facilities and open
spaces should be naturalized using native plantings.
Landscape buffers are required along arterial frontages
and where adjacent to residential uses to reduce visual
and operational impacts. Future planned developments
are encouraged to incorporate low-impact development
and green infrastructure practices to minimize any
environmental impacts of impervious surfaces and
stormwater runoff.

Conservation/Protected
This designation includes environmentally sensitive areas
that are protected by state and federal regulations, in
addition to areas that should be considered for additional
protection on a case-by-case basis, to the greatest extent
feasible. This designation includes areas within the
Ohio EPA Max Stream Corridor Setback, wetlands,
highly erodible soils due to steep slopes, wooded areas
of greater than three acres in size, prominent tree rows,
and other areas that are important for protection to
allow for the creation of linkages among conservation
areas. Additional sensitive areas not currently mapped or
protected by regulation, which may be identified through
engineering surveys, should also be considered for
protection, mitigation, or restoration.

                   The Big Darby Creek is one of Plain City's most

                   protections to preserve the remarkable biodiversity
                   of the creek and its surroundings.

RECOMMENDATIONS
STRENGTHEN OUR HOMES & NEIGHBORHOODS



These recommendations guide how Plain City plans for housing and invests in its
neighborhoods to support a growing and evolving community. They focus on expanding
housing choice, maintaining and enhancing existing neighborhoods, and ensuring
new development is connected, walkable, and aligned with available infrastructure and
services. By coordinating housing, land use, and infrastructure decisions, the Village can
support long-term sustainability, strengthen neighborhood character, and create places
that meet the needs of residents at all stages of life.

        2.2 Sweeney Run & West Avenue Focus Area
        Explore land use, transportation, and infrastructure
        strategies for the Sweeney Run and West Avenue area
        to support well-planned residential growth and a mix of
        housing types.

        The Sweeney Run and West Avenue area represents one
        of Plain City’s most significant opportunities to shape
        how the Village grows over the next decade. Located at
        the edge of Uptown and directly connected to a future
        trail and greenway spine, this area has the potential
        to become a model for how new neighborhoods can
                                                                     Sweeney Run is the location of the former
        support walkability, expand housing choice, and reinforce    Plain City Airport. The Airport was established
        community character.                                         in 1946 and operated for roughly 40 years.

        To guide this growth, the Village should advance coordinated concept plans for both Sweeney Run and
        West Avenue that establish a clear framework for land use, mobility, open space, and development patterns.
        These concept plans move beyond existing subdivision approaches in Plain City by organizing development
        around connected streets, integrated green space, and a mix of housing types that respond to evolving
        market demands.

        At Sweeney Run, the visionary diagram envisions a neighborhood structured around a continuous greenway
        corridor, where trails, open space, and natural features become the organizing elements of the community.
        Housing frontage should be built to face these spaces, encouraging an active and visible public realm, while
        strengthening connections to the broader trail network and Uptown. This approach not only enhances
        quality of life for residents but also creates a destination that draws people from across the Village.

        Along West Avenue, the concept introduces a different but complementary housing pattern, including
        townhomes and compact residential formats organized around shared courtyards and internal open spaces.
        These configurations provide additional housing diversity while maintaining a strong sense of community
        and walkability. Smaller lot sizes and attached housing types can help expand access to homeownership and
        offer alternatives for residents seeking lower-maintenance living options.

        The proximity of both areas to Uptown is a defining advantage. Future residents will be within walking or
        biking distance of shops, dining, parks, and community events, supporting an active lifestyle and reinforcing
        Uptown as the center of daily life. At the same time, these neighborhoods can help generate new foot traffic
        and economic activity that benefits local businesses and strengthens the Village’s core. Infill development
        is often accompanied by future thoroughfare planning and investments in safer streets and pedestrian
        infrastructure. This is especially important as vehicular traffic continues to increase through Uptown.
        Neighborhood-oriented infill development often reinforces pedestrian-focused streets, and over time
        influences vehicular behavior, prompting investment into upgraded travel lanes and intersections.

        Through concept planning, the Village can align infrastructure investment, ensure connectivity, and establish
        development patterns that prioritize people, open space, and long-term value. This includes coordinating
        utilities, street networks, and trail connections early in the process to avoid fragmented or inefficient
        development.

        As Plain City continues to grow, the Sweeney Run and West Avenue Focus Areas can serve as a model for
        future neighborhoods, demonstrating how thoughtful planning, diverse housing, and strong connections to
        open space and Uptown can create places that are livable and lasting.

2.3 Missing Middle & Small-Lot Zoning Package
Update zoning to encourage townhouses, duplexes,
quadplexes, and small-lot homes to expand housing
options and improve affordability.

Missing middle housing provides options for residents
who may not be served by traditional single-family
homes or large-scale multi-family developments. These
housing types, including duplexes, townhomes, cottage
courts, and accessory dwellings units (ADUs), can fit
within existing neighborhood contexts while increasing
housing choice and flexibility.

Today, Plain City allows some of these formats only
conditionally, while others, such as 3-4 unit building
and small-scale multi-family, are more restricted. Larger
                                                               Today, Plain City has a limited supply of missing-middle
minimum lot sizes and relatively low maximum lot                     housing. During the first Community Open House,
coverage in several districts also limit the feasibility of      residents were asked to select images that reflect the
smaller, more attainable housing types.                           types of housing they would like to see in the Village.
                                                              This input will help to shape the preferred housing types
                                                                                                and styles for the future.
Plain City should evaluate its zoning code to reduce
these barriers and introduce targeted updates that
expand where and how missing middle units can be
built. This may include reducing minimum lot sizes,
increasing allowable lot coverage, simplifying approvals
for duplexes and ADUs, and permitting small multi-unit
buildings in appropriate areas.

Clear design standards and examples should accompany
these updates to ensure new development remains
compatible with the Village’s character while supporting
a more diverse and attainable housing supply.



Definitions:

Small Lot Zoning Packages: Small lot zoning packages          Missing Middle Housing: The range of medium-density,
are typically introduced to allow higher density within       house-scale residential buildings that bridge the gap between
a single lot. This results in increased housing supply and    single-family homes and larger multi-family developments.
density as well as affordability. Components of a package     These housing types include duplexes, triplexes, townhomes,
include the allowing of accessory dwelling units (ADUs),      and courtyard apartments, designed to be compatible in scale

2.4 Uptown Living Initiative
Encourage new housing in Uptown to support local
businesses and increase daily activity.

Expanding housing opportunities in Uptown can help
reinforce its role as the heart of the community while
creating a unique living experience not found elsewhere
in the Village. Living in Uptown offers a blend of urban
convenience and small-town charm, where residents can
walk to shops, restaurants, parks, and community events
while remaining connected to a close-knit community.

Additional residents within walking distance of local
destinations help support small businesses, increase foot
traffic, and create a more active and vibrant environment
                                                                             Main Street Georgetown MD
throughout the day and evening. This consistent presence
                                                                           Source: Missing Middle Housing
of people not only strengthens the local economy but
also enhances safety, energy, and overall sense of place.

The Village should encourage upper-story residential,
small-scale infill, and mixed-use development that
integrates housing into the existing Uptown fabric.
This includes identifying opportunity sites, supporting
adaptive reuse of existing buildings, and ensuring new
development contributes to a walkable, engaging
public realm.

By creating more opportunities to live in Uptown, Plain
City can foster an active, connected lifestyle where
daily needs are within reach, and community life is
experienced just outside the front door.

environment. By growing local jobs, attracting essential
big-box style development, and supporting small
businesses in strategic locations, Plain City can capture
more employment, retain spending locally, and build a
stronger, more resilient economic base.

residential growth with jobs and business activity. They focus on supporting small
businesses, attracting employers, and creating vibrant places where people can work,
shop, and gather. By aligning economic development with land use, infrastructure, and
community priorities, the Village can strengthen its tax base, expand local opportunities,
and create a “live-work” community that supports long-term economic sustainability.

        3.2 Implement the Creekview Commerce Park Plan
        Creekview Commerce Park is one of the Village’s clearest opportunities to convert regional economic
        momentum into lasting local benefit. As Central Ohio continues to grow, Plain City is facing increasing
        pressure for new housing and development. The Village has also made clear that long-term fiscal health
        depends on more than residential expansion alone. Plain City’s own public guidance notes that maintaining
        a balanced, financially sustainable community requires attracting industrial development that creates jobs
        with living wages, and that the community has historically lacked sufficient sites for this kind of growth.
        Creekview begins to address that gap.

        The Creekview Commerce Park should therefore be treated as more than a future development site.
        It should be advanced as a master-planned business park with the capacity to diversify the Village’s
        economic base, provide shovel-ready sites, attract right-fit employers, and create new opportunities for
        both local residents and the broader community. The Village has already framed the project in these terms,
        emphasizing its potential to capitalize on recent large regional projects, align with local and state target
        industries, and generate substantial income tax revenue for Plain City.

        Implementation should remain closely tied to the qualities that distinguish Creekview from a conventional
        industrial project. The Village and its partners should continue to position the site as a high-quality, well-
        buffered employment district with strong development controls, durable design expectations, meaningful
        open space preservation, and a clear commitment to compatibility with nearby properties and the Big Darby
        Creek landscape. That includes following through on the project’s intended campus-like character, its
        extensive edge buffering, its internal trail and amenity framework, and its emphasis on attracting businesses
        that are a long-term fit for Plain City rather than simply filling land quickly.

        Just as important, Creekview should be pursued
        with a clear municipal value framework. Success
        should not be measured only by buildings
        constructed. It should be measured by the
        extent to which the project expands payroll,
        increases the number of quality jobs within
        Village boundaries, supports complementary
        commercial services, and improves Plain
        City’s long-term fiscal capacity. The Village’s
        incentive policy already points in this direction
        by prioritizing projects that create jobs, produce
        payroll, and add meaningfully to the local tax
        base.

        In that sense, Creekview is not simply
        a development project. It is a strategic
        implementation district that can help Plain            The Village at Hendrix in Conway, AR demonstrates a
        City capture more of the upside of regional             walkable, mixed-use model integrating employment,
        growth while maintaining stronger control over               housing, retail, and green space, supporting job
        design, infrastructure, and long-term community       creation, economic activity, and a vibrant, amenity-rich
                                                                                    environment. Source: DPZ Design
        outcomes. The project’s scale, location, and
        evolving entitlement status make it one of the
        most important economic development actions
        in the Plan Update.

Why Jobs Matter Fiscally in Plain City
The Village’s primary source of revenue is a 1.5% income
tax that generates about $3.8 million annually, covering
roughly 70% of the operating budget.

In Ohio, municipalities do not operate like counties,
townships, or school districts. Their most important
locally controlled revenue source is often the municipal
income tax, which means that attracting and retaining
jobs inside municipal boundaries can have an outsized
impact on long-term fiscal capacity. For Plain City, that
makes employment growth more than an economic
development objective. It is also a core fiscal strategy.

Other municipal revenue sources matter too. Property
                                                             Imperial Business Park, Source: The Silverman Group
tax revenues support local government in more limited
and structured ways than many residents assume, and
municipalities typically share that tax base with schools,
counties, and other jurisdictions. Development-related
revenues such as permit fees, plan review fees, utility
connection charges, and impact fees can help offset the
cost of growth, but they are often episodic rather than
long-term operating revenue. Municipalities may also
use tools such as community reinvestment areas, tax
increment financing, special assessments, and payment
in lieu of taxes (PILOT)-style arrangements to shape
fiscal outcomes or recover value from development under
certain conditions.

The practical point for Plain City is simple: not all
growth contributes to the Village in the same way. Land
uses that generate substantial employment and payroll        Van Aken District, Source: MKSK
can strengthen the income tax base and help support
services, infrastructure, and reinvestment over time. That
is why this Plan Update places a strong emphasis on
jobs attraction, business retention, and careful alignment
of annexation and incentive policy with the Village’s
long-term fiscal interests. The Village’s annexation
incentive framework already points in this direction and
can be sharpened further through job-oriented policy
alignment.

RECOMMENDATIONS
EXPAND & CARE FOR OUR PARKS



These recommendations guide how Plain City expands, connects, and maintains its
system of parks, trails, and natural areas to support a growing community. They focus on
improving access to open space, enhancing existing parks, and creating a more connected
network of recreational and environmental assets across the Village. By aligning park
planning with growth, infrastructure, and conservation priorities, Plain City can ensure
that all residents have access to high-quality open space while preserving the natural
features that define the community’s character and quality of life.

4.3 Pastime Park & Bicentennial Park Reinvestment
Reinvest in Pastime Park and Bicentennial Park to
enhance amenities, connectivity, and everyday usability
for residents of all ages.

As two of Plain City’s most well-used and recognizable
parks, Pastime Park and Bicentennial Park represent
the core of the community’s recreational life. Continued
reinvestment should focus on updating aging amenities,
improving accessibility, and enhancing connections
within and between the parks and surrounding
neighborhoods. Opportunities may include upgraded
playgrounds, improved pedestrian pathways, expanded
seating and gathering areas, and enhanced wayfinding.
Strengthening these parks as welcoming, flexible, and
easy-to-use spaces will help ensure they continue to
serve residents of all ages while accommodating growing
demand and evolving recreational needs.

4.7 Trails & Greenway Spine
Build a comprehensive trail and greenway network that
links neighborhoods, parks, and Uptown.

A connected trail and greenway network is a
foundational element of Plain City’s vision for a
healthy, active, and accessible community. By linking
neighborhoods, parks, schools, and Uptown, this system
will support recreation, alternative transportation, and
environmental stewardship across the Village while
improving access to everyday destinations.

The network should prioritize connections that link
key community assets and regional destinations, while
addressing gaps in existing sidewalks, bike facilities,
and off-road trails. Particular attention should be given       In 2024, Plain City added a new trailhead with walking

and connect trails
Creating a safe, complete, and connected transportation
network is essential to supporting Plain City’s growth
and everyday quality of life. As the Village continues
to evolve, how people move through and between
neighborhoods, schools, parks, Uptown, and job centers
will shape both accessibility and community character.
Plain City’s strategy is to build a transportation system
that works for everyone—linking local destinations
while connecting to the broader regional trail network so       The multimodal accommodations and walkable nature
                                                               of Uptown expand access between neighborhoods and
people of all ages and abilities can travel comfortably by              destinations, including parks, restaurants, and
foot, bike, mobility device, car, and even farm equipment.                                               regional trails.

in areas experiencing new development. Improving              as the community grows. A more connected system
connectivity within and between neighborhoods is              supports healthier lifestyles, reduces reliance on driving,
critical to ensuring that residents can safely access daily   and enhances the overall livability of the Village. The
needs, whether they're walking to a park, biking to           recommendations in this section provide a framework
school, or reaching Uptown’s businesses and services.         for building a transportation network that is safe, flexible,

These recommendations guide how Plain City improves mobility, safety, and
connectivity across the Village as it grows. They focus on closing gaps in sidewalks and
trails, enhancing key corridors, and creating safer, more comfortable routes between
neighborhoods and everyday destinations. By coordinating transportation investments
with land use and development, the Village can create a more accessible and efficient
network that supports all users, strengthens connections to community destinations, and
expands transportation choices for residents.

Existing and Proposed Trails
Plain City's existing trail network is limited, constraining
safe and convenient multimodal travel options. Most
of the Village lacks continuous pedestrian and bicycle
infrastructure, making it difficult to access parks,
neighborhoods, and natural areas safely and comfortably
without a vehicle. This gap in connectivity is particularly
evident in the limited number of off-street paths and
the absence of a direct link to regional trail systems,
restricting opportunities for both daily mobility and
recreational use.

Several proposed bike routes and trails shown on Figure
15 demonstrate the Village's emphasis on improving
connectivity. Planned on-road bike routes, shared use
paths, natural surface trails, and development-driven trail
systems will expand the network across the community.
A key opportunity is the potential extension of the
Heritage Trail into Plain City, which would establish
a critical connection to the broader Central Ohio
greenway system. These planned improvements represent
an important step toward creating a more complete, safe,            SR 161
and accessible trail network that better supports both
transportation and recreation.

        5.4 Feasibility Study for Uptown Bypass
        Evaluate the feasibility of a potential Uptown bypass to improve traffic flow, enhance safety, and reduce
        through-traffic impacts in the Village's core.

        As Plain City continues to gain residents, managing traffic through Uptown will become increasingly
        important to maintain safety, mobility, and community character. A feasibility study for a potential Uptown
        bypass offers an opportunity to evaluate whether redirecting through-traffic, particularly regional and freight
        traffic, could reduce congestion and conflicts
        within the Village core.

        The concept of a bypass is not new to Plain
        City. Previous planning efforts, including the
        2009 Thoroughfare Plan, identified the potential
        for alternative roadway connections to help
        redirect regional traffic around Uptown. This
        idea remains relevant today, particularly as
        development activity increases across the SR 161
        corridor and surrounding areas. Recent traffic
        analysis continues to highlight the physical
        constraints of widening SR 161 through
        Uptown, suggesting that additional connections
        or bypass routes may be a more feasible long-
        term strategy for managing regional traffic and
        preserving the function and character of the
        Village core.                                                           Christmas Under the Clock is Plain City's
                                                                             annual tree lighting ceremony, one of many
                                                                          community events in Uptown. The celebration
        This study should assess current and projected                     brings the community together with vendors,
        traffic patterns, including the volume and type                     food trucks, activities, and a holiday parade.
        of vehicles traveling through Uptown, and
        evaluate potential alternative routes or bypass alignments, including those previously identified that could
        accommodate through-traffic more efficiently. Consideration should also be given to how a bypass could
        impact local access, economic activity, and the overall function of Uptown as a destination.

        Successful implementation of a study will require partnerships with the Ohio Department of Transportation
        (ODOT), Mid-Ohio Regional Planning Commission (MORPC), and engineering consultants to
        identify feasible alignments, design alternatives, and potential improvements. Similar efforts have been
        pursued by the Licking County Transportation Improvement District in response to the arrival of Intel
        and surrounding development. The study identified priority improvements, including roadway repaving,
        widening, roundabout construction, and intersection realignments.

        In addition to traffic performance, the study should explore potential environmental, land use, and
        infrastructure implications, including right-of-way needs, cost considerations, and coordination with
        regional transportation agencies. Community input will be essential to understand concerns, priorities, and
        potential trade-offs associated with a bypass.

        By proactively studying the feasibility of an Uptown bypass, Plain City can better position itself to manage
        growth, improve safety, and preserve the character and function of its historic core.

        * Note: This recommendation is focused on evaluation rather than implementation. The goal is to provide the
        information needed to make informed decisions about long-term transportation investments and strategies.

URBAN TYPOLOGY:
UPTOWN SIGNATURE
Signature roads within the Uptown district where most activity is concentrated, these
roads exhibit a strong sense of place and identity. They support vehicular traffic flow and
provide a comfortable and inviting pedestrian experience.



The Uptown Signature typology supports the Village's
lively Uptown district, introducing elements that reflect
Plain City's identity and elevate the area's appearance.
These streets should be well-lit, multimodal, and lush
with street trees and native landscaping. Well-designed
streets within Uptown help maintain the Village's small
town charm, establishing a quaint and welcoming feel for
visitors to shop, dine, and gather in the district.

The Uptown Signature typology is applied to segments
of Main Street, Chillicothe Street, and Gay Street in
the heart of Uptown. The intersection of these three
streets are the focal point of the Village, used daily for
travel, activity, and year-round community events. Local      Main Street, Source: Google Earth
restaurants, shops, gathering places, and nearby parks
generate significant activity within this core. At the
same time, Main Street and Chillicothe Street are key
community thoroughfares that continue beyond the
community and link to neighboring destinations like
Columbus, Dublin, West Jefferson, and Hilliard.

The Uptown Signature street segments today are
functional, however, small improvements can refresh
safety and aesthetics. Existing enhancements, like
streetscape plantings and decorative banners, form
the foundation for an inviting experience for Uptown
patrons. Maintaining the vehicular flow of these roads
and incorporating more pedestrian-focused elements is
vital to creating a pleasant experience for all visitors to
the Village.                                                  Chillicothe Street, Source: Google Earth

The Uptown Signature road typology represents some
of Plain City's most iconic and memorable streets. These
streets are often the setting for community events like
parades, markets, and festivals, making identity and
community pride a central component of the proposed
Uptown Signature character. Seasonal decorations
including banners, flowers, and holiday lights can be
easily incorporated into the streetscape year-round.
Wayfinding signage in and around Uptown along major
routes can help visitors navigate the district and direct                                 Downtown Granville, OH
more foot traffic to businesses. Building a cohesive,               Source: Granville Area Chamber of Commerce
consistent identity throughout the public realm ensures
Uptown remains a hub of pride for the community.

To further support vibrancy and activity in Uptown,
businesses within the district are encouraged to extend
their activity onto the street. Outdoor dining, sidewalk
sales, and window displays all create a more enticing
Uptown experience, inviting visitors to spend more time
in the district and contributing to a healthier, livelier
community core.

Balancing pedestrian experiences with vehicular access is
critical for Uptown Signature Streets. With Main Street
and Chillicothe Street being highly-traveled arterial
roads that support truck and vehicular traffic, streets
need to be adequately designed not only to ensure traffic                          George St, New Brunswick. NJ

remains smooth and delays are minimized, but to avoid
disrupting the overall Uptown experience. Maintaining
turn lanes at intersections and signalized pedestrian
crossings can help facilitate vehicular movement and
reduce points of conflict within Uptown.

URBAN TYPOLOGY:
TRADITIONAL RESIDENTIAL
Historic Village streets that support compact development patterns and a mix of
residential and neighborhood-scale commercial uses. Buildings are typically oriented
close to the street, reinforcing a walkable environment within and near the Village core.



Traditional Residential streets support a dense mix
of homes, small businesses, and civic uses while
accommodating on-street parking and pedestrian
movement. These streets honor the historic
neighborhood development pattern surrounding
Uptown. Garages and parking areas are typically
accessed through rear alleys, allowing for a more timeless
neighborhood appearance along primary roads.

Existing Traditional Residential streets vary widely in
design. The two streets pictured on this page represent
the broad spectrum of existing conditions found on
residential streets near Uptown. Gay Street features
recent improvements that incorporate striped on-             Gay Street, Source: Google Earth
street parking, planted bump-outs, new sidewalks, and
a curb-and-gutter system to collect stormwater. The
street was converted to one-way traffic as part of these
improvements. By contrast, Shepper Avenue is a curbless
street that allows two-way traffic with unmarked on-
street parking and no sidewalks.

More cohesion among the various Traditional
Residential streets in the Village core can reinforce
identity and community, promoting walkability and a
more pleasant experience for residents and businesses.
These streets should maintain on-street parking access,
but should also provide pedestrians. While space is
limited due to buildings constructed close to roads,
targeted enhancements similar to those seen on Gay
Street can create a lasting impact on the neighborhood.      Shepper Avenue, Source: Google Earth

the small town charm that so many Plain City residents
want to see preserved as the Village grows. Designing
streets to protect this historic fabric helps maintain
the timeless appeal of Uptown and its surrounding
neighborhoods. These streets should complement the
Uptown Signature typology, utilizing similar design
elements like plantings and light poles to extend the
Uptown identity to residential areas.

URBAN TYPOLOGY:
TRADITIONAL ALLEY
Narrow through roads that provide rear access to homes and businesses, allowing parking
and loading activity to occur away from primary thoroughfares.




Vehicular access throughout the historic Village core is
aided by a network of alleys that allow circulation for
rear-facing driveways, garages, parking lots and pads,
or deliveries. These alleys generally do not support
continuous two-way traffic, but most currently allow for
bi-directional access due to their low traffic volumes.
While these alleys may not be frequented by visitors,
they are a key component of the Uptown identity, and
should be designed to support local circulation.

Some residential streets may be classified as alleys,
even if they do not have "alley" in their names, due
to the narrow width and overall function of the road.
Designating these roads as alleys alleviates the need      Center Street, Source: Google Earth
for them to meet the conditions desired for typical
residential streets, as many may not have the necessary
right-of-way to incorporate desired pedestrian
accommodations or on-street parking spaces.

Alleys in Plain City are a unique remnant of the
Village's past, and should be maintained and uplifted
as functional access roads for residents in the historic
Village core. While some streetscape elements like street
trees and sidewalks might not be feasible, alleys can still
play a valuable role in defining Plain City's identity.
Ensuring the Village's alleys remain clean, well-kept,
and accessible to residents helps keep other roads in the
urban core functioning properly.
                                                                          Updated residential alley, Fort Wayne, IN

compared to other roads, Traditional Alleys can still be

SUBURBAN TYPOLOGY:
COMMUNITY COLLECTOR
Streets that link residential neighborhoods to community destinations such as parks,
schools, and civic buildings. Comfortable pedestrian pathways, bike facilities, and traffic
calming measures allow all community members to utilize these roads safely.



Community Collector streets support traffic from
various neighborhoods while providing safe pedestrian
and bicycle routes and supporting access to homes
and businesses. Uses along these streets typically
include homes, civic centers, and neighborhood-
serving businesses. These roads also connect to various
neighborhoods throughout Plain City and provide access
to regional transportation networks. Their role as a link
between neighborhoods and destinations means they
need to facilitate moderate amounts of vehicular traffic
and provide pedestrian facilities near community assets.

Community Collector segments typically lead to
community facilities like parks, schools, and the Plain     Chillicothe Street near Pastime Park, Source: Google Earth
City Municipal Building, though they also connect to
neighborhood commercial areas. Multimodal traffic is
supported by sidewalks and "sharrows" designating lanes
to be shared by vehicles and cyclists.

Community Collector streets should be accessible
for all modes of transportation while maintaining a
neighborhood feel for residents and businesses. By
providing street trees, separate bicycle facilities, and
right-sized roads, the Community Collector typology
can provide a neighborhood roadway for all users that
minimizes dangerous driving and provides comfortable
options for active transportation.
