SUBURBAN TYPOLOGY:
BUSINESS PARK TRANSITIONAL
Connector streets that link major commuter routes and residential neighborhoods to
commercial and industrial business districts outside of the Village core.




With the potential for a new mixed-use district in the
Creekview Commerce Park, Business Park Transitional
streets can help ease the transition from adjacent
residential areas into a commercial setting that integrates
with surrounding neighborhoods. This roadway typology
does not exist in Plain City today, but multiple existing
segments and proposed future roads could embody this
type of road in the Village.

The existing segments designated as Business Park
Transitional segments are along Butler Avenue and
Converse Road in the northeast quadrant of Plain City.
These roads today are very rural in character, with narrow
lanes and low traffic volumes. Ensuring these roads, and      Converse Road, Source: Google Earth
any new roads, can accommodate commuter traffic to the
business district will minimize disruptions and ensure
successful community growth.

Business Park Transitional roads should be calm yet
efficient, with minimal curb cuts and consolidated
access points to simplify traffic flow. These roads should
feature plenty of trees, native plantings, and green
spaces to maintain a balance between development and
naturalized areas. The goal of this road typology is to
ease the transition from residential areas to employment
centers and create a pleasant atmosphere for all users.

SUBURBAN TYPOLOGY:
SUBURBAN RESIDENTIAL
Neighborhood streets serving lower density subdivision-style development with primarily
residential uses and a timeless community character.




Suburban Residential streets are distinct from the
Traditional Residential typology seen in the Village
center due to larger home setbacks, wider rights-of-way,
and more consistent, uniform standards for roadway
designs and development patterns. They are calm,
quiet streets that provide local access to homes while
accommodating on-street parking and sidewalks for
neighborhood pedestrian activity. Homes are typically
set back farther from the road with front driveway
access. Pedestrian pathways connect households
to neighborhood parks and schools, embodying a
communal character that supports the tight-knit feel of
these neighborhoods.
                                                             Alderwood Circle, Source: Google Earth
Many of Plain City's roads fall under the Suburban
Residential typology. These road designs are the most
consistent and uniform across the Village, but it is
critical for Plain City to continue enforcing high-quality
road design standards in all existing and new residential
neighborhoods to ensure consistent end products that
meet all users' needs.

RURAL TYPOLOGY:
GATEWAY ARTERIAL
Major entry corridors that create a recognizable and welcoming arrival experience into
Plain City. These routes balance high traffic volumes with enhanced landscaping, signage,
and design elements that reinforce community identity.



Gateway Arterial streets mark the approach to Plain
City, supporting traffic flow while creating visual
indicators that introduce the Village to visitors and
commuters entering via primary corridors. This typology
is concentrated on segments that support the most
traffic, particularly where commuters travel to other
major employment centers in the region. These roads
balance traffic management with community identity to
create a gateway experience that is distinctly Plain City.

Gateway Arterials in the Village include SR 161 east of
Butler Avenue and Plain City-Georgesville Road south
of Darby Fields Boulevard. These two segments mark
critical entryways to the Village, connecting to larger      SR 161, Source: Google Earth
communities like Columbus, Dublin, and Hilliard. Many
commuters and visitors use these routes to travel to and
from Plain City.

The existing character of these roads is distinctly rural,
with single drive lanes in each direction and naturalized
edges. Pedestrian pathways have been installed far
from the roadway in limited areas as part of suburban
development. As primary gateways to the community,
Gateway Arterial roads have the opportunity to create
a more distinct, welcoming approach to Plain City
that honors the Village's legacy and personality while
enhancing driver and pedestrian experiences.

RURAL TYPOLOGY:
RURAL COMMUTER
Major corridors that connect Plain City to surrounding communities and the regional
road network. These routes are primarily used for commuting, freight movement, and
longer-distance travel while maintaining a rural roadway character.



Rural Commuter corridors allow efficient and
continuous traffic flow with access to neighborhoods
concentrated at few intersections to reduce congestion
caused by turning vehicles. These roads are some of the
most heavily used routes in the Village. They feature
larger setbacks from the roadway and wide shoulders
to allow farm equipment to travel safely next to higher
speed vehicles.

Rural Commuter road segments in Plain City include
all of US 42 and parts of SR 161 west of US 42. These
routes extend far beyond the Village, connecting
Plain City to the broader Central Ohio region. These
routes have limited pedestrian facilities that are often     US 42/Jefferson Avenue, Source: Google Earth
unprotected, with sidewalks built directly next to
vehicular lanes. Restaurants, retail centers, and civic
buildings are located along these roads, with some
residential homes built along SR 161.

As major arterial roads through the Village, Rural
Commuter roads prioritize efficient and safe traffic flow.
However, with several popular community destinations
and retail centers along these roads, providing
accommodations for pedestrians and cyclists to access
businesses and civic buildings can transform these roads
into more complete streets that accommodate all modes
of travel.

RURAL TYPOLOGY:
RURAL RESIDENTIAL
Low-traffic roads serving very low density housing, farmland, and rural properties. These
roads provide access to rural homes, farms, and agricultural operations.




Rural Residential roads are located at the edges of the
community extending outside Village limits and connect
rural areas to the broader road network. They support low
traffic volumes and sometimes permit higher speeds due
to their low-density development patterns and straight
geometry. Properties along these roads often feature
large setbacks, long entry drives, and very low density,
reinforcing a natural, agricultural environment.

Existing Rural Residential roads in and around the
Village include Cemetery Pike, Converse Huff Road,
and Lafayette-Plain City Road. These roads connect
to major arterial roads in the area as well as various
suburban neighborhoods in Plain City, tying the              Converse Huff Road, Source: Google Earth
Village's road network to other regional locations via
low-traffic country roads.

Delivery trucks, farm equipment, and personal vehicles
use Rural Residential roads to access homes, businesses,
and farms in the outskirts of the Village. On Cemetery
Pike, bike route signs direct cyclists to the access point
for the Heritage Trail. Any pedestrians and cyclists who
wish to use these routes to access regional trails, or who
simply want to walk or bike along the road, must share
the right-of-way with motorized vehicles.

Rural Residential roads are meant to exhibit the idyllic
scenery of the countryside surrounding Plain City.
Unlike the urban and suburban residential typologies,
where road striping isn't necessary, Rural Residential
roads should include painted striping that indicates
where vehicles are allowed to pass.

For pedestrians and cyclists who want to use these
roads, a shared use path allows a safer, more inviting
option for non-motorized travel. These paths can create                                       New Albany, OH
a highly-valued recreational asset for the community,                                 Source: Randall Schieber
allowing residents and visitors to actively explore the
scenic outskirts of Plain City on a dedicated trail,
potentially connecting to other regional trails and nearby
recreational facilities like the Heritage Trail or various
Village parks. High-visibility crosswalks near recreational
facilities can help ease access to parks and trails.

As growth within the Village approaches these rural
edges, traffic management may become a greater concern
for residents and workers who use these roads. To
preserve the rural character and prevent congestion on
Rural Residential roads, traffic should be directed to use
primary arterials roads whenever possible. The Village
may explore strategic locations to install roundabouts at
Village gateways or entries to suburban neighborhoods
where traffic delays are likely. Using roundabouts in lieu                             The Cannery, Davis, CA

of stop signs or traffic lights can keep traffic flowing
smoothly and reduce overall congestion without the need
to add additional lanes to Rural Residential roads.

These recommendations guide how Plain City strengthens Uptown as a vibrant, active,
and economically resilient destination. They focus on supporting local businesses,
encouraging a mix of uses, enhancing public spaces, and improving walkability and access.
By coordinating public investment with private development and ongoing programming,
the Village can reinforce Uptown as a year-round destination that supports community
life, attracts visitors, and sustains long-term economic vitality.



6.1 Additional Community Space
Expanding public gathering spaces in Uptown or the
surrounding area will increase the social and civic
identity that already exists today. Recent investments,
including the Depot at Public Square completed in May
2025, along with planned additions such as The Park at
Public Square and The Marketplace at Public Square, are
creating a vibrant hub where residents and visitors of all
ages can gather.

These spaces, along with additional pocket parks, plazas,
and multi-use indoor facilities, can host events, markets,
performances, and community programs, providing
flexible environments that support a wide range of
activities. Looking ahead, the Village will also need to
consider larger or more adaptable gathering spaces that            The grand opening at the Depot at Public Square

                                                                The Uptown Public Space & Events Spine is more than
A public space network is essential to activating Uptown        a collection of places; it is a community hub for social
as a year‑round destination and the heart of Plain City.        interaction, cultural expression, and economic vitality.
The Uptown Public Space & Events Spine envisions a
coordinated series of parks, plazas, streets, and gathering
venues that not only serve recreational needs but also
provide flexible space for community events, markets,
performances, and civic gatherings.

This network builds on existing and proposed assets
including the projects at Public Square and other
planned improvements, while emphasizing connectivity
to unite these spaces as one cohesive system. The spine
should weave together spaces for everyday use (such
as small plazas and pocket parks) with larger venues
capable of hosting festivals, concerts, and community
celebrations. Together, these elements create a rhythm of
activity that draws people through Uptown and supports
local businesses.

including seasonal markets, outdoor movie nights, car
shows, holiday lighting events, community caravans,
parades, and other local and cultural celebrations will
further activate the spine and extend Uptown’s appeal
throughout the year—from Main Street, to the public
square, to Pastime Park, and beyond.

The public space network should be designed with
flexibility in mind, allowing spaces to function
independently for daily use or collectively for larger
community events. Design considerations such as
seating, shelter, lighting, and utilities should support ease
of use for both planned and spontaneous activities.

Implementation of this spine will require coordinated
planning among the Village, landowners, local
businesses, and community groups. Key priorities
include identifying opportunities to expand public
space where gaps exist, securing rights or easements for
connectivity, and leveraging event programming as a tool
for economic and social activation. Funding strategies

Identify target project opportunities to attract investment
and revitalization in Uptown.

Strategically identify and promote key redevelopment
sites in Uptown to help guide investment and support
long-term revitalization. These efforts should focus on
underutilized or highly visible properties where targeted
improvements can create momentum and encourage
additional private investment.

Catalytic projects should prioritize a mix of uses that
bring consistent activity throughout the day, including
residential, retail, dining, and office or service-based
businesses. This mix can help generate steady foot traffic,

7.4 Coordinate with Utility Partners for Land Use &
Capital Planning
Create tools to assess current service offerings and
identify expansion plans that align with anticipated
development.

These tools provide clarity for developers, staff, and
service providers by illustrating where and how growth
can be supported. A service coverage map should identify
existing and planned water and sewer service areas,
including capacity and the timing of system expansions
in coordination with Mid-Ohio Water & Sewer District.
This allows users to understand where infrastructure is in
place and where upgrades or extensions may be required.

Together, these resources help define infrastructure
readiness by distinguishing areas that are development-
ready from those that require additional investment.
They also support a more predictable and efficient
development review process, shifting from reactive,
case-by-case decisions to a clearer, more coordinated
approach.

The Service Coverage Map and Growth Review
Checklist also support implementation of the
Public Safety & Civic Services Capacity Plan
(Recommendation 7.2) by helping identify service gaps,
prioritize infrastructure improvements, and align growth
with available capacity (see maps of sewer coverage and
Mid-Ohio Water and Sewer District projects on page
70-72 of the Conditions and Trends Report in Appendix
A).

These tools should be maintained as a living resource,
updated regularly to reflect changes in service capacity,
infrastructure investment, and development processes.

        IMPLEMENTATION
        This chapter identifies priorities, partnerships, and
        tools that will help Plain City translate the plan’s
        goals into coordinated decisions and investments
        The Comprehensive Plan provides a vision and set of recommendations
        for Plain City’s future, but its success ultimately depends on consistent
        implementation and ongoing collaboration. This chapter focuses on how
        the Village can move from planning to action by identifying next steps,
        establishing priorities, and outlining the roles that staff, elected officials,
        community partners, and residents will play in carrying the plan forward.

        Implementation is an ongoing process that requires coordination across
        departments, boards and commissions, regional partners, and the broader
        community. As decisions are made about development, infrastructure
        improvements, parks, housing, and public services, the plan should serve as a
        guide for evaluating opportunities and aligning projects with the community’s
        shared goals. By working together and maintaining a long-term perspective,
        the Village can ensure that individual decisions contribute to broader
        community outcomes.

        The Comprehensive Plan will also help inform future planning efforts and
        investment decisions. It can guide updates to local policies and regulations,
        support capital improvement planning, and help prioritize projects that
        strengthen infrastructure, enhance public spaces, and support economic
        development. Using the plan as a reference point for budgeting, programming,
        and long-term investments will help ensure that growth is managed
        thoughtfully and resources are directed toward the community’s most
        important priorities.

        Implementation should also be viewed as an adaptive process. As conditions
        change and new opportunities emerge, the Village should periodically revisit
        the plan, track progress on key initiatives, and make adjustments when needed.
        Regular follow-up, coordination among partners, and continued community
        engagement will help keep the plan relevant and ensure that Plain City
        continues to move toward its vision for a resilient, vibrant, and connected
        future.

IMPLEMENTATION 179


INTRODUCTION
The Plain City Comprehensive Plan was created for
the community and is intended to be used by Village
staff, Council, boards and commissions, and community
partners as they make decisions about the future of the
Village. The updated plan represents an important step
forward, positioning Plain City to manage growth while
addressing both emerging challenges and long-standing
community priorities.

This plan provides a framework to guide Plain City’s
evolution into a connected and inclusive community
that meets the needs of all residents through thoughtful
urban design, strategic investment, and people-
centered solutions in housing, economic development,
and transportation. By establishing clear goals and
recommendations, the plan helps ensure that decisions
                                                            Stakeholder Focus Group – an early collaboration effort
about development, infrastructure, and community
                                                               to gather input from business owners, residents, and
investment support the Village’s long-term vision.             local organizations about community challenges and
                                                              opportunities, helping to shape both the engagement
This chapter focuses on how the Comprehensive Plan                       process and the final outcomes of the plan.
can be used as an ongoing guide for decision-making. It
outlines how the Village can incorporate the plan into
daily operations, coordinate future planning initiatives,
and track progress toward key community goals. It also
highlights the importance of aligning the plan with
capital improvement planning, policy updates, and long-
term investment decisions.

Through regular monitoring, collaboration across
departments and partners, and periodic updates,
the Comprehensive Plan can remain a practical and
adaptable tool. By using the plan as a shared reference
point, Plain City can continue advancing its goals while
protecting the character, values, and sense of place that
define the community.

PUTTING THE PLAN TO WORK
Using the Plan
This Comprehensive Plan Update should be referenced
as part of daily operations as public and private decisions
are made concerning land use, development, capital
improvements, economic development, and other key
topics. Village staff familiar with the Comprehensive
Plan can introduce other department staff, boards,
and commissions to the document and train them on
how best to utilize it. Future Village planning efforts,
including capital improvement planning, strategic
planning, and focus area planning, should align with the
Plan. Additionally, the Village and staff should continue
to collaborate and hold planning workshops with their
departments and stakeholders to ensure that efforts
continue to align with their goals.

Monitoring the Plan
Regular review and monitoring of the plan
recommendations will help track implementation and
                                                              Village Council members Jamey Sintz and Tyler Harriman
produce tangible outcomes. Plan review should happen               engage with residents and local business owners at a
at a designated time no less than once per year. The               Community Caravan open house, demonstrating how
plan review should result in an annual progress report,        Village staff’s active involvement and collaboration help
which can be shared with the community and Council.             ensure the Comprehensive Plan is practical, achievable,
                                                                                    and responsive to community needs.
The metrics provided within the implementation tables
for each topic area can be used as key indicators for
monitoring plan progress and success.

Update the Plan
This Comprehensive Plan Update is intended to be
durable and thorough, while still providing flexibility for
the Village and community partners to implement the
Comprehensive Plan to the best of their ability. Despite
this, a plan is a snapshot in time, and as change occurs,
the Plan will need to adapt to keep the community’s
vision in mind.

and lasting change. Many actions require coordination

when financial, legal, or other constraints limit the

    Breaking it Down…
    The items below provide an overview on reading and understanding the components of the implementation matrix.

    1. Plan Pillar: Pillars are major focus areas that represent an important dimension of Plain City's future, organize
       the plan’s recommendations, and reflect the community’s long-term priorities.

    2. Goal: The goal statement is an aspirational statement that describes a desired future or outcome. Each section has
       an accompanying goal statement.

    3. Recommendation: An action identifies a specific step the community can take to advance the Plan’s goals. Each
       recommendation is numbered according to the order in which it appears in Chapter 3 (e.g. 1.1, 1.2, and so on).

    4. Type: Identifies the nature of the action, such as a policy, project, program, plan, or other recommended approach.

    5. Lead: The Lead refers to the primary Village department that will spearhead each effort. In many cases, there may
       also be supporting departments or outside partners involved in carrying it through. (Note: Abbreviations are used
       and can be found in the legend on the following page.)

    6. Support: The organizations and groups listed in this column are Village boards and commissions, institutions, or
       other community groups that can be involved in implementing the plan recommendations. (Note: Abbreviations are
       used in many cases and can be found in the legend on the previous page.)

    7. Timing: Indicates whether an action is specific and time-bound or an ongoing policy directive.

    8. Priority: The priority indicator is used to call special attention to recommendations identified as being very
       important to the community during the planning process. (Note: Council may choose to shift priorities annually over
       time, in response to community desires and preferences.)

City’s long-term vision.

SUMMARY + NEXT STEPS
The Implementation chapter provides the essential link
between Plain City’s vision and real-world outcomes. It
serves as a practical guide for staff, councils, commissions,
and community partners, offering clear steps to apply,
monitor, and refine the plan’s recommendations over
time. This plan emphasizes collaboration and shared
responsibility, recognizing that achieving many actions
requires coordination beyond the Village’s direct control.

Built on extensive conversations with staff, stakeholders,
and residents, this chapter reflects the community’s
priorities and insights, ensuring that implementation
strategies are responsive, actionable, and grounded in
local context. By using the guidance in this chapter, Plain
City can take ownership of initiatives, track progress
through defined metrics, and adapt as circumstances
change, ensuring the Comprehensive Plan remains a
living document that continues to advance the Village’s
long-term goals.

Working Together:
Bringing the plan’s ideas to life will require strong
partnerships and continued collaboration across
the community. While the Plain City Departments
and Divisions will play a central role in leading and
coordinating many initiatives, lasting success depends
on the involvement of key partners, public agencies,
neighboring communities, institutions, organizations,
and residents working together toward shared goals.
These partnerships help ensure that projects are both
visionary and achievable, aligning resources, expertise,
and community priorities.




192 PLAIN CITY COMPREHENSIVE PLAN


The Picture Plain City Comprehensive Plan update captures an exciting
moment in time for our community. Yet, like any picture, it represents only a
single snapshot. The hours continue to pass, and our Village continues to evolve.

This final plan is the result of countless hours of work, surveys, conversations,
and community touchpoints. Its development created meaningful
opportunities for residents to engage with the Village’s operations, and my
hope is to carry that momentum forward in the years ahead as we bring
this plan to life. With the final recommendations, the administration of this
community has been tasked with developing new and better relationships,
investing more than ever in the infrastructure of the Village, and continuing
our goal of connecting each resident with amenities – both with physical trails
and streets and in new opportunities for recreation and services. We take this
responsibility seriously.

This document is meant to grow with us. It is a living plan; one that will be
revisited and refined as new challenges emerge and new opportunities take
shape. While the landmarks and faces within the Village may change over
time, the character and spirit of Plain City remain constant. And just as the
hands of the historic Clock Tower continue their steady movement forward,
the Village Administration, Mayor, and Council will continue adapting to the
times to best serve the residents and businesses that make this community
exceptional.



				                                  - Haley Lupton, Village Administrator

                                                                                 Conditions and Trends Report | 5


Why Update the Comprehensive Plan?
In the midst of growth and change, Plain City is preparing for the future, while protecting
what makes Plain City special.
+ Strategic Growth: Guide new development in a way that reflects community values and maintains the
  village’s small-town character.

+ Infrastructure Investment: Align land use and infrastructure improvements—like water and sewer
  upgrades—to support sustainable, long-term growth.

+ Economic Development: Position Plain City to attract new businesses, support existing ones, and create
  a strong local economy.

+ City Status Readiness: Plan for the transition to city status by 2030 with the services, governance, and
  amenities to match.

+ Regional Leadership: Strengthen Plain City’s role in the growing Central Ohio region by planning
  intentionally for opportunity and change.




A. Introduction                                                                              Conditions and Trends Report | 6


Community Context
+ Plain City is located at the western edge of the Columbus Metropolitan Area, one of the fastest-
  growing regions in the Midwest. The village is experiencing significant residential and commercial
  development as development pressure from the greater Columbus area moves westward. Despite
  recent growth, Plain City retains a distinct small-town character rooted in its historic Uptown core,
  strong agricultural heritage, and scenic rural landscapes.

+ Regional connectivity is key. U.S. Route 42, US-33, State Route 161, and I-270 provide direct
  access to regional job centers, with most major employment hubs less than a 45-minute commute.
  This accessibility positions Plain City as both a desirable residential community and an emerging
  employment center.

+ The community is closely tied to its natural environment. Big Darby Creek, a nationally recognized
  scenic river, flows through the village and provides both a unique recreational amenity and an
  environmental stewardship responsibility. Protecting this natural resource while accommodating
  growth is a key priority for the community.

+ Plain City is at a pivotal moment. Recent projects and plans underscore the village’s efforts to
  balance growth with preservation of community character. Together, these efforts envision a future
  where Plain City serves as both a thriving residential destination and a vibrant local economy that
  reflects its heritage, identity, and regional role.

   B. Key Findings                                                            Conditions and Trends Report | 11


Key Findings
From Rural Roots to Rapid Growth...
+ Once a quiet village in Central Ohio, Plain City
  has undergone a profound transformation in
  the past two decades. Since 2000, Plain City’s
  population has nearly doubled, growing from just
  over 2,000 residents in 2000 to nearly 5,000
  today.

+ Plain City functions largely as a bedroom
  community, with 96% of residents commuting
  elsewhere for work and only 8.3% of local jobs
  filled by residents. This imbalance places added
  demand on local services and amenities without
  capturing the full benefit of employment growth.

+ Housing construction, which slowed following
  the Great Recession, has since exploded. 895
  new housing units were permitted in the past five
  years, nearly all of them single-family homes.


B. Key Findings                                       Conditions and Trends Report | 12


Key Findings
From Rural Roots to Rapid Growth...
+ Plain City’s housing market has experienced
  significant appreciation. Home values have more
  than doubled since 2000, rising over $200,000
  in median value, outpacing nearby communities.
  The rising cost reflects both growing demand and
  limited supply of housing.

+ Great schools, employment proximity, and
  available land all contribute to housing demand
  in Plain City. Central Ohio’s development
  community is increasingly looking west, where
  projects can be delivered more quickly, at lower
  cost.

+ Job creation has not kept pace with population
  growth. Jobs growth has stagnated since
  2012, and nearby closures such as RANCO in
  2004 has impacted growth in complementary
  manufacturing jobs.

B. Key Findings                                      Conditions and Trends Report | 13


Key Findings
A Community in Motion...
+ Plain City is well-positioned within a booming
  metropolitan region. As Central Ohio expands
  toward a projected population of 3.15 million
  by 2050, Plain City’s role is shifting from rural
  crossroads to a maturing small town. The village is
  seeing sustained residential growth, infrastructure
  upgrades, and increasing development pressure.

+ Infrastructure investments are reshaping the
  development landscape. Major upgrades to water
  and sewer systems are already underway, led by
  the Mid-Ohio Water and Sewer District, which
  now maintains and operates Plain City’s water
  and wastewater facilities. These improvements are
  essential to meeting environmental standards and
  supporting future capacity.




B. Key Findings                                         Conditions and Trends Report | 14


Key Findings
A Community in Motion...
+ Uptown Plain City, the community’s historic core,
  continues its revitalization efforts guided by the
  2018 Comprehensive Plan and the 2023 Uptown
  Master Plan. Key efforts include Main Street
  streetscape enhancements, expanded public
  spaces, and infill development. These projects aim
  to preserve the village’s identity while adapting to
  growth.

+ At the same time, Plain City is investing in the
  quality of life. Public services, park amenities,
  and trail systems are being expanded. Community
  pride remains strong, with residents valuing
  traditions, civic events, and natural features like
  Big Darby Creek. These investments and amenities
  now face the challenge of keeping pace with the
  expectations of a growing population.



B. Key Findings                                          Conditions and Trends Report | 15


Key Findings
Looking Ahead...
+ Plain City is projected to exceed 5,000 residents
  by 2030, slated to become a city under Ohio law.
  This milestone will mark more than a change in
  municipal status, it reflects the community’s long-
  term evolution and increasing regional influence.

+ The next phase of growth will bring both
  opportunity and complexity. As housing costs rise
  and population diversifies, the Village will need
  to address issues of affordability, job growth, and
  adequate delivery of services. Upgrading facilities
  and staffing, expanding housing types, attracting
  local employment, enhancing transportation
  infrastructure, and multi-modal connections are all
  key topics to contemplate.

   C. Regional Conditions                                                        Conditions and Trends Report | 19


Regional Dynamics
         Mid-Ohio Water Sewer District (MOWSD)
         Established in 2023, the MOWSD will improve sewer infrastructure and oversee water
         distribution, operation, and treatment in Plain City and parts of Madison County. Future
         expansion of county-wide water and wastewater lines will have major impacts on Madison
         County’s growth potential.

         Emerging Regional Employment and Industry Sectors
         Many companies are establishing logistics facilities, manufacturing, and data centers in Central
         Ohio. Most of these job centers are within a 45-minute commute from Plain City. Examples
         include Intel in Licking County, Amazon Web Services in Union County, retail distribution
         centers in West Jefferson, EV investments in Fayette County, and recently announced Anduril in
         Pickaway County.

         Big Darby Creek Protections
         The 2024 update to Ohio EPA’s State Water Quality Management (208) Plan, specifically
         Appendix 9-3, extends Darby-related permit requirements beyond Franklin County, applying
         them to all counties within the Big Darby watershed. Additionally, pollutant discharge into Big
         Darby Creek is reaching its regulatory limit, which sparked a region-wide solution for future
         growth in Madison County.
                                                                                       Conditions
                                                                                       Conditions and
                                                                                                  and Trends
                                                                                                      Trends Report
                                                                                                             Report || 20
                                                                                                                       20
 C. Regional Conditions


Regional Dynamics
         Regional Housing Shortage
         Housing construction in the region has not kept pace with job growth, particularly in Franklin
         County. This shortage contributes to sharp increases in housing prices and land value
         throughout the region. As a result, development pressure has shifted further out to rural
         counties, like Madison and Union Counties, where land prices are more affordable and large-
         acre parcels are readily available. Combined with future water and sewer improvements along
         US-42 and SR-161, Madison County is positioned to absorb growth as one of the few remaining
         underdeveloped counties in the metro.

         Zoning, Policy, and Infrastructure Updates Across the Region
         Many communities across the region are preparing for projected growth by updating zoning
         regulations and policy documents. For example, Columbus is modernizing its major road
         corridors holistically to jumpstart urban housing development. In July 2024, they introduced
         “ZoneIn” districts along major corridors that allow for higher densities and building heights.
         Additionally, COTA’s LinkUS program aims to deliver Bus Rapid Transit lines along high-capacity
         corridors like West Broad Street and West Main Street. Nearby local governments, like the City
         of Dublin and Jerome Township, are also exploring ways to provide meaningful connections
         between neighboring communities through roadway, parks, and trails investments.

MOWSD Projects
                                        Map 07 | Proposed Mid-Ohio FPA




Mid-Ohio’s proposed 5-year
sewer service area enables
substantial growth along S.R.
161 and US-42.
It is anticipated that some of the
resulting development enabled
by centralized utilities may
request annexation into Plain City.
However, areas not contiguous
to Plain City’s boundaries may
develop within unincorporated
areas of Madison County. These
investments threaten the village’s
ability to control growth responsibly
and prevent incompatible uses.

   D. Conditions Analysis                                                 Conditions and Trends Report | 31


Demographics & Workforce
Key Findings
+ Plain City is growing rapidly. The village is on track to reach city status by 2030
  (>5,000), reflecting sustained residential and population growth.

+ Increase in families and school-aged children. Rising enrollment in Jonathan Alder Local
  School District point to an increase in the number of families with children moving to
  Plain City.

+ Most of Plain City’s residents work elsewhere. Growth in new housing has increased this
  dynamic; attracting new residents from nearby communities.

+ Jobs in Plain City are not held by local residents. This indicates a mismatch between job
  types, their respective wages, and the education attainment of residents.

+ Household income is rising faster than the region. Since 2000, median income has
  doubled—outpacing trends in both Union and Madison Counties.

Jobs available in Plain City are not the types of jobs that
are held by residents.
+ Educational attainment among Plain City’s
  residents is generally higher than that of its
  workforce. 34.3% hold a bachelor’s degree
  or higher, compared to just 16.6% of the local
  workforce. This gap reflects how residential growth
  has attracted highly educated residents who
  often work elsewhere, while local employment
  opportunities remain limited in high-skill, high-
  paying positions.

D. Conditions Analysis                                                         Conditions and Trends Report | 36


Housing & Neighborhoods
Key Findings
+ Housing costs in Plain City are among the highest in Madison
  County. Prices have continued to rise in recent years, resembling
  new housing starts found in Dublin and Jerome Township.

+ Nearly one-third of housing units in Plain City are rental units.
  Most are smaller structures with fewer than 10 units.

+ However, most new residential units are traditional single-family.
  Multi-unit buildings continue to age, and diversity in housing types
  are declining.

+ Plain City’s housing stock shows a widening age gap. The
  largest shares are in homes built before 1939 and post-2020, with
  comparatively little mid-century housing in between.

+ Most residents own their homes. Over 75% of housing units are
  owner-occupied.

D. Conditions Analysis                                                                                Conditions and Trends Report | 42


Land Use, Development, & Conservation
Key Findings
+ The village grew around 882 acres since
  2022, a 56% increase. Growth is driven
  primarily by new residential land uses,
  located primarily along the southern and
  eastern portions of the village.

+ Plain City and the surrounding area is a
  prime market for residential development.
  Availability of large land areas surrounding
  the village, proximity to regional employment
  centers, and potential future wastewater
  availability along key arterials all contribute
  to the growing development pressure inside
  and surrounding Plain City.




   D. Conditions Analysis                           Conditions and Trends Report | 43


Land Use, Development, & Conservation
Key Findings
+ Conservation principles are at the forefront of
  new development. Open space and stormwater
  management are facilitated through the village’s
  development review process and updated Ohio
  EPA policies.

+ Planned Unit Development (PUD) Districts
  are commonly used for newly annexed
  developments. The Planned Unit Development
  District is the village’s primary tool to facilitate
  quality, master planned development.

+ As the village looks ahead, it continues
  to explore tools to manage growth and
  development effectively. Tools like are available
  to support neighboring local governments,
  fund infrastructure improvements, and provide
  amenities for residents.

Uptown Plan & Progress
Key Findings
Goals from the 2023 Uptown Plan
1. Create a Diverse and Vital Economy - Promote new
   business, reduce vacancy, and increase retail presence via
   incentives, programs, and marketing.
2. Mix Compatible Land Uses - Increase population density
   and residential opportunities to improve safety and enhance
   function of Uptown.
3. Strengthen Identity - Make Uptown an inviting place within
   the community using branding and wayfinding strategies
   such as signage, streetscaping, and public art.
4. Enhance Mobility - Improve safety and access in Uptown
   with bike amenities, pedestrian pathways, and wayfinding.
5. Promote Design, Art, Culture, and History - Capitalize on
   Uptown’s cultural heritage by holding more events and
   increasing civic and cultural land uses.

Water & Utilities
Key Findings
+ Plain City’s water and wastewater
  infrastructure is now operated by the Mid-
  Ohio Water and Sewer District. The creation
  of the District was prompted by regional
  growth, limitations on future discharges to
  Big Darby Creek, and the need to modernize
  aging infrastructure.

+ Environmental regulations and continued
  population growth are driving significant
  infrastructure investments. The village’s
  existing wastewater treatment facility
  discharges to Big Darby Creek, a high-quality
  waterway subject to heightened Ohio EPA
  standards. These regulations necessitate
  ongoing upgrades to meet stricter water
  quality requirements.
  D. Conditions Analysis                          Conditions and Trends Report | 68


Water & Utilities
Key Findings
+ The Mid-Ohio Water and Sewer District
  will lead future sewer infrastructure
  improvements. This includes assuming
  ownership and operational responsibilities,
  modernizing legacy systems to meet current
  and projected demand, and constructing new
  sewer lines along OH-161 and US-42.

+ Marysville’s sewer infrastructure may play
  a role in supporting future growth along
  primary corridors in Union County. Marysville
  currently operates a sewer line along US-42,
  which could potentially serve development in
  unincorporated Union County as well as areas
  that may annex into Plain City.

Parks, Recreation, & Open Space
Key Findings
+ Pastime Park is the village’s primary recreation
  hub. It hosts most outdoor events and amenities,
  highlighting the need for expansion or improvements
  to prevent overuse.

+ More than half of Plain City’s population lives
  within a 15-minute walk of a park. This indicates
  a good level of access to green space across the
  village.

+ Two new parks will enhance access and relieve
  pressure on existing spaces. The Jackson Street
  Dog Park and McKitrick Nature Preserve will expand
  the village’s recreation network, offering new
  amenities and reducing reliance on Pastime Park as
  the community’s sole major destination.

  D. Conditions Analysis                                                                                                                                                                                       79


Governance
Key Findings
+ Plain City’s 2021 home rule charter formalizes a governance structure designed for
  city status. It establishes a Mayor-Council-Administrator model that distributes authority
  between elected leaders and an appointed administrator.

+ Several boards, commissions, and volunteer committees support local decision-
  making. These groups cover a wide range of topics and reflect strong civic involvement.

+ Plain City has broad control over village operations. However, the village has limited
  direct control over certain essential services that fall under county authority.

+ Plain City is split between two counties. With differing rules, funding priorities, and
  systems between Union and Madison Counties may lead to different development
  patterns.

D. Conditions Analysis                                                                                     Conditions and Trends Report | 81


Several boards, commissions, and volunteer committees support local decision-making.
+ Economic Development Committee – Provides recommendations and guidance to
  village Council on policies, programs, and initiatives related to economic development.
+ Parks and Recreation Committee – Oversees planning, development, and
  maintenance of parks and recreation facilities, identifies gaps and needs in local
  related services, and advocates for these changes to village leadership.
+ Personnel and Finance Community Improvement Plan Committee – Facilitates
  coordination between personnel matters, financial resources, and capital improvement
  needs, works with the Finance Department and makes recommendations on
  expenditures.
+ Board of Zoning Appeals – Reviews and decides on requests related to land use,
  building setback, height restrictions, and other zoning-related matters.
+ Planning & Zoning Commission – Oversees a wide range of development activities
  and land use processes, such as development reviews, rezoning applications, and
  conditional use approvals.
+ Personnel Board of Appeals – Reviews personnel disputes submitted by village
  employees and uses policies, procedures, and law to decide on a case’s ruling.

D. Conditions Analysis                                                       Conditions and Trends Report | 82


Plain City is split between two counties – Differing rules, funding priorities, and systems
between Union and Madison Counties may lead to inconsistent development patterns.

+ Zoning and development must account for
  county-specific regulations, utility service
  areas and providers, or roads, which could
  lead to differing growth patterns across
  the county line.

+ Residents in each county may experience
  variations in property tax assessments,
  health mandates, or county programming.

+ Differences in county investment
  priorities (such as infrastructure or social
  services) may contribute to perceived or
  actual inequities within the community.

+ The availability of county-level data,
  resources, and technical assistance may
  differ.

Round 1 Emerging Themes
Engagement efforts from August to October 2025 revealed important insights from the community, and several
recurring themes emerged from this round.

        Preserve Agricultural Land                                     Grow Local Services & Amenities

   Strong desire to preserve farmland and maintain the            Interest in more essential services like a grocery store
   village’s semi-rural surroundings.                             and pharmacy while keeping the small-town feel.


        Expand Community Gathering & Recreation                        Protect Natural Assets

   Invest in park improvements and other public spaces,           Protect the biodiversity of the Big Darby Creek and
   community events, and recreation opportunities.                other natural resources from future development.


        Improve Connectivity & Mobility                                Balance Growth with Preservation

   Expand sidewalk coverage to enable safe pedestrian and         Focus on growth and development that enhances
   bicycle travel. Connect Plain City to the greater regional     livability without compromising Plain City’s small town
   bikeways system.                                               charm.

        Manage Housing Development                                     Build on the Uptown Momentum

   Opinions toward housing are mixed, but the majority are        Support for mixed-use infill that enhances local retail and
   against significant housing development, particularly multi-   dining options while maintaining historic character.
   family housing.

Engagement Round 1: Key Takeaways
The following takeaways highlight what residents value about Plain City and where they see
opportunities for growth and improvement. Understanding these priorities will help guide the
Comprehensive Plan Update and ensure that the plan reflects the community’s long-term vision.

1. Preserve and elevate natural and recreational assets. Residents value the village’s natural
landscapes, parks, and the Big Darby Creek ecosystem.
  + Key takeaway: Prioritize environmental conservation and park investment as a foundation of
    future land use.

2. Manage growth to protect small town and rural character. Residents expressed concerns about
losing Plain City’s small town charm to suburban-style sprawl or high-density development.
  + Key takeaway: Prioritize context-sensitive infill, protect agricultural land, and reinforce the
    historic core. Align land use planning and policies with these values.

3. Strengthen connectivity and safety. The village lacks pedestrian and bicycle access between
neighborhoods, parks, schools, and Uptown.
  + Key takeaway: Develop safety improvements like pedestrian crossings, roundabouts at high-
    traffic intersections, sidewalks, and trail linkages.

                                                                                          Engagement Summary | 13


Engagement Round 1: Key Takeaways
4. Support local retail and essential services. Residents want more amenities and conveniences
such as a grocery store, pharmacy, and retail without turning the city into a commercial hub.
 + Key takeaway: Seek opportunities for neighborhood-scale commercial and mixed-use
   nodes. Pursue local retail and dining that aligns with village character over large modern
   developments.

5. Balance housing needs with community values. Many residents oppose large multi-family
developments but some are open to limited development of single-family, mixed-use or
diverse housing types if they fit the village character and help maintain
affordability.
 + Key takeaway: Develop a housing strategy that expands options
   through design-sensitive infill and prioritizes single-family over multi-
   family.

Engagement Round 2: Key Takeaways
The following takeaways highlight what residents value about Plain City and where they see
opportunities for growth and improvement. Resident’s feedback on initial recommendations can
ensure that the plan reflects the community’s long-term vision.

1. Preserve and elevate natural and recreational assets. Residents value the village’s natural
landscapes, parks, and the Big Darby Creek ecosystem.
  + Key takeaway: Develop strong policies that support environmental conservation and highlight
    park investment as a foundation of future land use.

2. Manage growth to protect small town and rural character. Residents expressed concerns about
losing Plain City’s small town charm to suburban-style sprawl or high-density development.
  + Key takeaway: Prioritize context-sensitive infill, protect agricultural land, and reinforce the
    historic core. Align land use planning and policies with these values.

3. Focus on community spaces. Residents appreciate the public spaces and community events that
exist, but they want more of these amenities.
  + Key takeaway: Invest in projects that bring the community together, take advantage of
    opportunities to build more public space, and prioritize family-friendly places.

                                                                                          Engagement Summary | 24


Engagement Round 2: Key Takeaways
4. Support local retail and essential services. Residents want more amenities and conveniences
such as a grocery store, pharmacy, and retail without turning the city into a commercial hub.
  + Key takeaway: Seek opportunities for neighborhood-scale commercial and mixed-use
    nodes. Pursue local retail and dining that aligns with village character over large modern
    developments.

5. Balance housing needs with community values. Many residents oppose large multi-family
developments but some are open to limited development of single-family, mixed-use or diverse
housing types if they fit the village character and help maintain affordability.
  + Key takeaway: Develop a housing strategy that expands options
    through design-sensitive infill and prioritizes single-family over multi-
    family.

5. Continue to engage with residents beyond the planning process.
Residents are eager to partake in planning processes and value feeling
heard.
  + Key takeaway: Create more outlets for civic engagement and let
    residents in on the “why” when making development decisions.

                                                                                                                        APPENDIX 310


MEMORANDUM

       To:    Members of the Village of Plain City Council
       From: Haley Lupton, Village Administrator
       Date: June 29, 2026
       RE:    Resolution 27-2026: Amending the Village of Plain City Employee Policies and
              Procedures Handbook



Background:

In routine review and inspection of the Village of Plain City Employee Policies and Procedures
Handbook, staff has identified several necessary revisions and has formally recommended the
implementation of such revisions. The proposed revisions are identified in Exhibit A as attached
to Resolution 27-2026. A brief summary of the proposed revisions is as follows:

   •   Section 4.4.4 (titled “Police Department Fitness Standard Incentive Program”): Creation of
       a new section that formalizes the implementation of a physical fitness incentive program
       for certain employees of the Plain City Police Department.
   •   Section 5.9 (titled “Unpaid Leave (Non-FMLA)”): Creation of a new section that addresses
       policies regarding unpaid personal leave.

Objective:

To approve and implement amendments to the Employee Policies and Procedures Handbook.

Recommendation:

Staff supports and recommends the passage of Resolution 27-2026 at the second reading on
August 10, 2026. The amendments to the Employee Policies and Procedures Handbook have been
reviewed by the Personnel and Finance, CIP Committee accordingly, with a formal
recommendation of approval received from the Committee. Staff is confident that the
amendment furthers the goals and objectives of Council, specifically regarding the goal of
“continual development of organizational professionalism”.




        800 Village Boulevard | P.O. Box 167 | Plain City, OH 43064 | 614-873-3527 | plaincityohio.gov


                              RESOLUTION NO. 27-2026

     A RESOLUTION AMENDING THE VILLAGE OF PLAIN CITY EMPLOYEE
                POLICIES AND PROCEDURES HANDBOOK

WHEREAS, the Village of Plain City Council previously approved Resolution 06-2026 which
implemented revisions to the Village of Plain City Employee Policies and Procedures
Handbook (the “Employee Policies and Procedures Handbook”); and

WHEREAS, the Employee Policies and Procedures Handbook is applicable to employees of
the Village of Plain City in order to provide a systematic and organized approach to the
establishment, implementation, and administration of the personnel policies and practices
relevant to all affected employees of the Village; and

WHEREAS, periodic reviews of the Village’s personnel policies and practices take place to
ensure compliance with state and federal labor laws and regulations and circumstances
that arise through the course of Village operations; and

WHEREAS, pursuant to the directives of the Village Council, amendments to the Employee
Policies and Procedures Handbook are proposed, as shown in Exhibit A attached hereto and
incorporated herein; and

WHEREAS, the Village Council has determined it necessary to amend the Employee Policies
and Procedures Handbook, as shown in Exhibit A attached hereto and incorporated herein.

NOW THEREFORE BE IT RESOLVED by the Council of the Village of Plain City, Ohio, a majority
of the members elected or appointed thereto concurring, as follows:

Section 1. The Village Council hereby approves and authorizes the amendment of the
Employee Policies and Procedures Handbook, as identified in Exhibit A and attached hereto
and incorporated herein, with the language being added is in red and underlined.

Section 2. The Village Administrator and Finance Director are hereby authorized and
directed to ensure the implementation of the amendments to the Employee Policies and
Procedures Handbook and obtain acknowledgement by employees of the Village of their
receipt of such amendments.

Section 3. It is found that all formal actions of this Council concerning and relating to the
passage of this Resolution were adopted in an open meeting of this Council and that all
deliberations of this Council that resulted in this formal action were in meetings open to the
public in compliance with all legal requirements, including Section 121.22 of the Ohio
Revised Code.

Section 4. This Resolution shall be effective from and after the earliest period provided by


law.

                      Introduction, Applicability and Administration

The provisions of the Village of Plain City Employee Policies and Procedures Handbook are
applicable to all employees, except as specifically provided herein. This Handbook’s
purpose is to provide a systematic and organized approach to the establishment,
implementation, and administration of the personnel policies and practices relevant to all
affected employees. This Handbook is not a contract of employment or a guarantee of any
rights or benefits, but is merely intended to be used to assist and guide employees in the
day-to-day direction and performance of their duties. Any promises or statements made by
any individual that conflicts with this Handbook is unauthorized, expressly disallowed, and
should not be relied upon.

The policies adopted in this Handbook supersede all previous written and unwritten
personnel policies or operational guidelines that directly conflict with this Handbook. All
previous written personnel policies or operational guidelines that do not conflict with this
Handbook shall continue in full force and effect. This Handbook is also intended to be
construed in such a manner as to comply with all applicable federal, state, and civil service
laws and regulations. Employees are responsible, as a condition of their employment, to
familiarize themselves with, and abide by, these policies and procedures.

The Village will endeavor to give employees advance notice of any Handbook changes.
However, the Village may revise these policies with or without advance notice. Notice of
revisions shall be provided to all employees. Employees are encouraged to make
suggestions for improvements in personnel policies and practices to their supervisors.

If any article or section of this Handbook is held to be invalid by operation of law, the
remainder of this Handbook and amendments thereto shall remain in force and effect.
Should a conflict arise between the Ohio Revised Code (O.R.C.) or applicable federal law and
this Handbook, law shall prevail. Additionally, should a direct conflict exist between this
Handbook and a Collective Bargaining Agreement, the Collective Bargaining Agreement
shall prevail.

                                                                             Village of Plain City
